Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Summoned By Congress Over Chinese Espionage Concerns (arstechnica.com) 8
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia's chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation. The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People's Republic of China's access to sensitive US technology and information," representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote. "The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk," the lawmakers added.
The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia's chips. Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," the company said. "Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information -- not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets -- and zero information relevant to national security," it added.
The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against "foreign adversary espionage." The company said its chief executive had an "outstanding security team" that travels with him. The New York Times said Huang had not received a "defensive briefing," which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity. Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.

Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
18:44:38 UTC
03:44:38 KST

Security researchers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access, potentially allowing outsiders to launch cyberattacks against unsuspecting targets.
The hacking software, called Artex, is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, and it’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July. As open source software, it’s free for anyone to download and run on their own servers, making it a popular tool for those who cannot access Anthropic or OpenAI’s most advanced cybersecurity AI models for discovering security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has previously described Artex as a system of AI agents that can conduct cyberattacks “from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction.”
In a blog post, cybersecurity firm Censys, which scans the internet for exposed or vulnerable systems, said that it identified more than 800 distinct deployments of Artex that were accessible from the web without needing a password to log in.
Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys who wrote the blog post, said that not every instance of Artex is operated maliciously and many are used for authorized testers. But it’s unclear why hundreds of these Artex systems are exposed to the web, as the software does not require them to be accessible from the internet.
The findings underscore how even powerful hacking tools can be misconfigured to be publicly accessible by anyone, increasing the chance that someone will find and misuse them. The publicly accessible systems also expose attack tools, such as implants (hidden malicious software) used to compromise and maintain persistent access to a victim’s network.
Security companies have linked the use of Artex to several broad-scale cyberattacks, including against the Korean finance industry in September. Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike attributed the attacks to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance in the attacks, in part because the hacker had left an “open directory” hosting the system. Censys said that its data showed the Artex instance in question had been publicly exposed for months, and appeared to contain more attack data that extended “well beyond South Korean banks,” including payment and gaming companies.
Artex was also used in an attack on IT support giant ConnectWise earlier in October, which allowed Chinese-linked hackers to spy on thousands of organizations whose data and files are hosted in Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft, which has visibility into the attack, said in a blog post that the hackers used Artex to break into customers’ cloud environments and steal their data at such speed that defenders had “little time to detect and respond.”
Many of the attacks linked to Artex involved exploiting simple vulnerabilities, such as guessing weak or known passwords, and a lack of multi-factor authentication.
The findings show that simple vulnerabilities, including misconfigurations, can expose both the attacker and their targets.
Artex has since announced it would go closed-source, effectively limiting further releases for paid customers. There are still dozens of copies of Artex’s code available on code-sharing sites that can still be used in active attacks.

Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.
As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.
For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.
“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.
Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.
“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.
On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”
Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.
The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice, which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.
The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot, which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.

Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
18:42:30 UTC
03:42:30 KST

A massive permitting bill that could help energy projects come online much quicker and potentially lower utility bills for Americans is advancing with bipartisan support. And while it could be a catalyst for lots of clean energy, it could also speed up polluting projects and limit oversight of new data centers.
Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
The Senate will vote to push through a giant — and controversial — permitting reform bill.
Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
The Senate will vote to push through a giant — and controversial — permitting reform bill.
With data centers demanding more electricity for AI, environmental advocates fear that developers could take advantage of the reforms to evade public scrutiny and rely more heavily on fossil fuels. The bill sacrifices caution for speed, limiting environmental reviews and preventing communities from stopping a project from moving forward by taking it to court.
“Whether it is permits to bulldoze wetlands, the fast-tracking of gas pipelines or general environmental review, with this legislation, data centers would not need to answer to the concerns of local communities,” Christy Goldfuss, executive director of the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), says in an email to The Verge. “People would be shocked to realize their representatives are rushing such a consequential decision.”
The bill sacrifices caution for speed
The sea change in Congress following the midterm elections could put the bill in an even more precarious position, giving Democrats a better shot at pushing for their priorities in the bill and potentially triggering a fight with President Donald Trump. Should it come up for a vote during the current lame-duck session or get kicked to next year, the bill will test whether Democrats and Republicans can actually get something done to address some of the biggest issues voters carried with them to the polls: rising energy costs and data centers encroaching on their communities.
“They swung big with this bill. It’s a really good bipartisan compromise,” Xan Fishman, executive vice president of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells The Verge.
Four senators calling themselves the “four corners” — Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) — introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on September 30th. “If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” Whitehouse, a climate hawk, said in the press release.
The announcement simultaneously garnered support from climate and renewable energy groups, as well as fossil fuel interests. “Pass the frickin’ bill so we can start building things again,” the US Oil & Gas Association said in a statement.
The Senate could vote to move the bill forward as early as next week, teeing it up for potential passage before the end of the year, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman expects President Trump will want to sign the bill if the current Republican-controlled Congress acts, adding in an email that the White House has been “very involved” in negotiations. Newly empowered Democrats, however, could decide to drag out debate on the bill until next year in order to make fewer concessions to Republicans.
“Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control.”
If it becomes law, the bill would limit the reach of bedrock laws (stemming back to the 1970s environmental movement) that protect water resources and endangered species and give the public an opportunity to weigh in on large projects that might impact public health. Over the years, however, reviews that once took months at most might take several years or even decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman attributes the delays largely to lengthy legal battles. Now, agencies have to spend more time preparing for lawsuits as they consider permitting applications, Fishman says. That holds up development on all kinds of infrastructure projects, including cleaner energy alternatives to fossil fuels.
Fishman expects BAAJA to be very effective in amending outdated permitting rules that have become burdensome to projects across the board, even those that might ultimately have a net positive impact on the environment. “Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control,” he says. “You want to protect the environment, you want to protect people, but you want to get to a yes or no [on a permit application] in a reasonable amount of time and you don’t want to have this endless litigation cycle.”
The bill would set a 45-day deadline for a lead agency to issue a decision on a project after completing an environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). In many cases, NEPA review is the only opportunity for nearby residents to weigh in on large projects that involve the federal government. And it’s been a key tool for opponents to high-profile projects including the Dakota Access and Keystone XL pipelines. BAAJA narrows the scope of projects subject to NEPA, creating exclusions for transmission upgrades and certain pipeline expansions, to name a couple. Many projects receiving federal loans or grants or that have already been through a similar state environmental assessment would no longer trigger NEPA review.
The bill also sets a strict new 150-day limit for anyone to challenge a project in court over alleged violations of NEPA, the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, or National Historic Preservation Act. And BAAJA strips away a court’s ability to halt a project altogether even if it finds that a federal agency violated NEPA; it would simply force the agency to correct any issues.
The Clean Water Act allows the Army Corps of Engineers to issue general permits to projects that discharge dredged material into US waters as long as they’re deemed as having “minimal adverse environmental effects.” BAAJA could make it easier for large projects including data centers to qualify for those permits.
Some environmental groups are concerned that those general permits would take away public participation requirements for individual projects, especially when it comes to data centers that use a lot of water. The proposals in BAAJA amount to “rubber-stamping permits under the Clean Water Act” and “blocking interference from States and Tribes,” according to the environmental organization Earthjustice Action.
“It will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out.”
They’re also concerned that BAAJA aligns with the Trump administration’s push to deregulate industry and weaken environmental protections in order to swiftly build out more data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure to power them. Data center energy demand has led to a surge of new gas projects in the US, and the bipartisan bill could help streamline reviews for new pipelines delivering fuel for data centers.
“One very big reason why passing BAAJA is such a high priority for the gas industry is it will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out,” Earthjustice Action President Abigail Dillen said in a Thursday blog. “BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers.”
Long pipeline delays slow data center development, according to energy research firm Wood Mackenzie. Permitting reform could benefit data center developers building out their own gas generation rather than relying solely on the grid, so-called “behind-the-meter” projects, by ending regulatory delays when it comes to connecting pipelines. Reforms would also speed grid-connected gas generation, Wood Mackenzie says in a recent news release.
“I don’t think we’re seeing it as this bill helping one type of technology over the other. I think it clears the way for all technologies to get onto the grid a little quicker,” Siddhant Warrier, research analyst for North American Power for Wood Mackenzie, tells The Verge.
Notably, the bill is supposed to protect bipartisan interests by preventing any single administration from attacking a particular project type — such as the Biden administration attempting to phase down oil and gas in the power sector or the Trump administration issuing stop work orders to wind farms. BAAJA aims to provide “project certainty” by barring federal agencies from canceling or suspending permits they’ve already approved in most cases. It even allows developers to take agencies to court for “disparate treatment” to sue for damages incurred from project delays.
“This part of the legislation could also lead to a slew of industry lawsuits that result in taxpayers paying billions of dollars to private industry,” the NRDC warns in its analysis of the bill. It could also prevent communities from challenging projects, including data centers, that wind up having unforeseen consequences for the environment and public health.
Despite those concerns, the NRDC and other advocacy groups are optimistic about the bill boosting renewable energy and enabling power grid upgrades needed to meet rising demand while keeping costs down.
BAAJA could shorten the time needed to build a new transmission line nearly in half — from 10 years or more to around five or six years, the NRDC estimates. Transmission lines that carry electricity across long distances — key to getting electrons to urban centers from far-flung solar and wind farms — are particularly tricky to build because of the patchwork of permitting processes they’re subject to across different jurisdictions.
Two separate reports project that the permitting bill would increase renewable energy capacity in the US and cut greenhouse gas emissions as a result. It also points to modest reductions in energy costs as a result of BAAJA passing compared to a baseline reflecting the status quo. The average annual cost of producing electricity would fall by as much as 7 percent by 2041, according to modeling by think tank Resources for the Future. Household electricity bills would lower by $50 to $78 per year by 2040, according to an analysis by research firm Rhodium Group. The White House put out its own analysis in October claiming that the average household could see their electricity bills fall by as much as $251 each year as a result of BAAJA.
One of the ways BAAJA aims to keep utility bills from rising is to force data center developers to pay more for transmission costs. Current law prevents utilities from charging them for costs stemming from both new builds and existing infrastructure, which inadvertently shifts costs to other customers to fill in the gap. The bipartisan bill mandates what’s called “and pricing” so that data centers and other large electricity customers would be on the hook to pay for both added and existing infrastructure.
The bill would also require utilities to disclose electricity sales to data centers. It would force large data center developers to make financial assurances to utilities before they break ground, as well as make them responsible for covering costs of new energy projects even if the data center shutters before the infrastructure is paid off.
Unfortunately, the bill may only solve part of the problem since utility rates reflect more than just transmission costs. Increasing electricity demand from the data center boom can still raise prices for fuel and gas turbines, for example. And the bill doesn’t address other issues that have sparked backlash against data centers, like noise and air pollution from generators on site.
Still, without permitting reform, gas and power prices would likely continue to climb as new energy projects keep hitting bottlenecks, according to Wood Mackenzie. Even environmental groups concerned about some of the provisions in BAAJA are holding out to see if Congress can amend the bill to strengthen environmental and consumer protections.
The bill has become a sort of Rorschach test for its backers, one expert speaking on background tells The Verge. They’re all optimistic that their energy source of choice, be it oil and gas or solar and wind, will ultimately come out on top — as long as it gets the green light to build.

Arkivism Is an Accessible Antidote to AI with 4 Million+ Public Domain Images

Arkivism Is an Accessible Antidote to AI with 4 Million+ Public Domain Images
Say you’re on the hunt for a drawing of a duck wearing a hat or a glimpse at Morocco in 1850 or a clip of people celebrating in the streets. Whatever imagery it is you’re searching for, Arkivism has likely got you covered.
An accessible antidote to generative AI, Arkivism is a new public domain index that catalogs millions of artworks, illustrations, photos, video, and more from dozens of museums and archives around the world. While many digital collections exist online, the “visual library of Alexandria,” as its creator dubs it, is searchable with a phrase, a mode of research that’s become commonplace with the proliferation of chatbots. Simply describe what you’re looking for and be presented with an array of human-made results.(via Open Culture)

Meta&#8217;s Muse AI can create custom &#8216;spaces&#8217; for the version of the app you need right now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
18:13:41 UTC
03:13:41 KST

Meta will now allow you to build customized, app-like experiences within Muse. The new feature, called “spaces,” allows its AI assistant to build things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, music tracker, trivia game, and more, which you can interact with directly in the Muse app.
Meta’s Muse AI can create custom ‘spaces’ for the version of the app you need right now
You can create things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, or music tracker directly within Muse.
Meta says you can create a new space by describing it. If you connect an outside app to Muse — like Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable, Notion, and others Muse works with — the AI assistant will continuously pull information from them, allowing it to update pricing, dates, and other information in your space in the background. You can also interact with elements inside your spaces by checking things off, adding notes, and making edits.
You can also change the placement of your spaces in the Muse app, too, as Meta lets you keep them in the sidebar, move them into your main tab, or schedule when you see them. “For example, keep your weekly planner up front during the workweek, then swap it for your weekend plans on Saturday,” Meta says.
Meta also announced that it’s bringing new “Active Memory” and “Active Focus” capabilities from its Muse Wonder AI model into the Muse app and its Meta AI chatbot. This will allow Muse to understand when past information becomes relevant during conversations, as well as make it better at working toward goals.
Meta is rolling out spaces to all Muse users. The company is also looking into ways to share your spaces with other users and collaborate with them.

We know 15k websites are infected. how do we tell them?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
18:13:35 GMT
03:13:35 KST

We've identified 15,579 websites that are currently infected with malicious JavaScript and between them, we conservatively estimate that they receive more than 135 million visits every month.
We know they're infected, and we have the evidence to back that up, but there's a problem: how on Earth do we tell them all?
As our Threat Intelligence capabilities at Report URI have grown, identifying compromised websites has become increasingly efficient. Unfortunately, responsible disclosure hasn't kept pace, and we're now finding infections considerably faster than we could ever hope to notify the affected organisations.
I genuinely don't know how to solve this problem, so I'm asking for help.
What attacks we're finding
At the core of it, we're finding websites that are running JavaScript that they should absolutely not be running! For some examples of how nasty this can be:
- Credit card skimmers - often known as 'Magecart', they target payment pages and skim full card details to send them to the attacker.
- ClickFix attacks - designed to trick users into completing a "prove you're human" challenge and instead installing malware on their device.
- Device exploitation - loading malware to compromise specific versions of iOS and install spyware, like DarkSword or Coruna.
- Redirects - these can send the visitor anywhere, including fake login pages to phish details, device security 'warnings', scams, and much more.
All of these are bad scenarios for the innocent visitor, and attackers change their payloads depending on their objective.
How these sites are compromised
There are many ways an attacker can get malicious JS onto a site, but here are the main categories that we group the initial vectors into from what we're seeing:
- Direct compromise - typically a WordPress vulnerability or similar, the site's own JS files are modified to include the malicious JS.
- Supply chain - a third-party script file that a site loads is infected with malware, and is then loaded on to the site, exposing all visitors.
- XSS - good old traditional XSS, a vulnerability in the site itself that allows JS to be injected.
- DeadTag - a threat group we named recently, buying expired domains that sites still load JS from, reviving them, and serving malware.
Unfortunately, there are a lot of different ways that this can go wrong, as we're seeing.
The scale of the problem
Right now, we have 15,579 unique sites that are infected with one of the malicious JS attacks listed above. Those are the sites where there is no doubt in our mind, and the list of sites where we have some suspicion but haven't got to 100% confidence is thousands more. Take September as an example, because we haven't quite finished processing everything from October yet, and this is the tally for new sites that we identified as being infected:
These are the sites that, as of today, are still infected. We remove sites once they clear their own infection as we have no concern about trying to notify them, so there were more than this.
In terms of traffic volumes, it's quite surprising how quickly this adds up. None of the sites in the list are global leaders, but we do have a huge presence of regional leaders. For example, if we look at .fr, .es and .de sites, some of them are really highly ranked sites in those countries, but they barely crack the Top 1 Million globally. Being a top site in France still gets you quite a hefty amount of traffic it turns out. Using various sources of data, and being ultra-conservative with our estimates, our list of currently infected sites is comfortably receiving a combined 135 million visits a month. That's a lot of exposure.
So, what do we do?
We continue to reach out directly to those sites that we identify as particularly high impact and try to notify them, though this is happening on an admittedly small scale. The process of responsible disclosure consumes a lot of resources, use of security.txt is low, and the vast majority of our emails and messages go unanswered. It's simply not possible for us to scale this up.
As these are sites we're crawling and identifying ourselves, we have no contact information like we would for a customer. So, as things currently stand, that's where we are, and I'd like to hear suggestions on what we can do.
If you're from an NCSC/CERT, especially in Europe where we seem to be finding a lot of impacted sites, please reach out to intel@report-uri.com and we'd be happy to provide a list of infected sites in your region. Hopefully you would be able to have more success in notifying the impacted sites than we would. 
If you're an organisation and believe having commercial access to our threat intelligence feeds would help you protect your own customers, you can also reach out to intel@report-uri.com for details.
Back to the original problem, though, and it pains me to say it but I don't have a clear idea on how we can try to have more of a positive impact. If you think there's something you can help with, an idea you'd like to put forward, or a suggestion on what we can do with all of this data, please drop by the comments below and I'd be happy to hear from you.
We have intelligence that could help protect millions of website visits, and we need help to turn it into action.
Update: 6th Nov 2026 21:36 UTC
A lot of questions have been raised across various social channels and especially the HN thread, so I thought I'd answer them in one central place:
Why hasn't the list of sites been published?
There are a few reasons:
- I didn't want this to be a 'name and shame' as the sites on that list are, after all, victims of attacks. Someone broke into their site, and the owners probably have no idea.
- If the list is widely disseminated and absorbed into blocklists, trying to get your domain of those lists afterwards is close to impossible. For a small business, that could be devastating.
- Many of these websites were likely infected because of an existing vulnerability that was exploited in something like WordPress, Magento or similar. Handing out a list of viable targets does not seem like a good idea.
Why not use the WHOIS contacts?
Since GDPR back in 2018, I've found that data to be mostly useless. What you get is either nothing, a registrar web form, or a relay address such as the Namecheap or GoDaddy privacy mailboxes. 
Why not contact the hosting providers?
Because so many of these sites are behind a CDN provider or other proxy service, so the IP resolution doesn't give any indication of who the hosting provider is to contact them. 
Why not just send an email to every website?
I could probably try to automate that, but to what email address? I'd have to hit a selection of common ones, info@, support@, abuse@, maybe others? There are also close to 16,000 of them, have you ever tried to send 16,000 emails? The manually curated emails have almost no response rate so a spammy mailshot seems unlikely to help, and could also trash my email reputation!

Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
18:03:33 UTC
03:03:33 KST

Computer Science > Machine Learning
  [Submitted on 15 Oct 2026 (v1), last revised 3 Nov 2026 (this version, v3)]
Title:Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent's earlier actions. For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window. However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model's context short remains challenging for existing systems. Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gathers information from an entire document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent 'memory tokens' for a frozen LLM. Memorilla encodes documents (such as user chats, book chapters) once into reusable embeddings, then learns to retrieve and place query-specific information in the LLM's input embedding space. Using only 16 memory tokens, Memorilla achieves the best performance against baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks spanning personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive question answering. Notably, on FactKG, it reaches 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference, while using 108x fewer tokens to represent the source documents. Furthermore, Memorilla can facilitate continual learning in agentic systems where the document count (the agent's past turns) increases throughout the trajectory. In a TextWorld environment, we show that Memorilla reduces the agent's tendency to wander between rooms it has already explored, and improves its average success rate from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%. Overall, Memorilla aids frozen LLMs in accumulating and using knowledge effectively across long-context interactions and takes a step towards building continually learning AI systems.

Kalshi court losses pile up as judges refuse to block state gambling laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
18:02:34 UTC
03:02:34 KST

Kalshi is having a bad week in the federal court system. Two circuit appeals courts rejected the prediction market’s latest attempts to block state gambling laws in Connecticut, New York, and Nevada. Kalshi is separately facing a new lawsuit filed by the Arkansas attorney general.
In all cases involving Kalshi and state governments around the US, the main issue is whether state gambling laws apply to prediction markets despite Kalshi’s claim that its platform offers “swaps” that can only be regulated by the US Commodity Futures Exchange (CFTC). The Trump administration is on Kalshi’s side, with Donald Trump Jr. serving as an advisor to Kalshi in exchange for a generous equity deal.
“Kalshi insists that its products are not gambling,” but “Arkansas law is concerned with substance, not semantics,” Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin said yesterday when announcing his lawsuit against Kalshi. Kalshi’s prediction market lets customers “wager money on the outcome of just about anything” despite the fact that “gambling on an unregulated platform is squarely prohibited by Arkansas law,” he said.
Griffin’s lawsuit was filed in an Arkansas state court. Kalshi violated state law by offering gambling to people as young as 18 and by failing to pay taxes or comply with other restrictions, Griffin said. Arkansas law permits gambling within certain limits, such as an age minimum of 21 years old for electronic wagering accounts.
“Instead of obtaining the licenses, submitting to the oversight, complying with the restrictions, and paying the taxes required of lawful gambling operators in Arkansas, Kalshi opened its platforms to Arkansas consumers, including individuals as young as 18 years old, encouraged them to wager real money on sporting and entertainment events, and profited from those wagers,” Griffin said.

Tesla to Wind Down Cybertruck Production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Tesla to Wind Down Cybertruck Production (cnbc.com) 149
			
		 	
				Elon Musk says Tesla will be "winding down" Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory around mid-2027 to free up capacity for increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi. CNBC reports:  The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company's plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward. Musk did not say whether the company would produce the Cybertruck at a different facility, but he later responded to a user on X who called the update an "end of an era" and said the Cybertruck was the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made." "True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time," Musk said.
The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk's pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000. "Trucks have been the same for a very long time," Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019. "Like 100 years. Trucks have been basically the same. We want to try something different." While Tesla does not break out its sales by model or region, Cox Automotive estimated sales of the Cybertruck last year at 20,237 units in the U.S., down 48% from 38,965 in 2024.  Thank you Slashdot reader Dan Posluns for sharing the news.

Perplexity launches AI agents for work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
17:59:41 UTC
02:59:41 KST

Teammates are agents for complex, ongoing work
Perplexity teammates coordinate AI agents, manage ongoing projects, and follow through across ops, marketing, and more.
Perplexity pioneered the first web-capable AI assistant in July 2025 in the Comet browser. It was useful for booking restaurants, shopping, and dozens of uses popular with personal agents today.
Since then, model capabilities have advanced dramatically. And Perplexity Computer is where millions of people and companies do serious work with accurate AI. Personal agents need to be purpose-built for work.
Today, we’re launching teammates, personal agents that can take on that long-running work. They plan and coordinate projects, switch gears as priorities change, and present results for review. Users can inspect and guide their work along the way.
Computer can handle complex projects, but setting up an agent to own ongoing work required planning. Teammates build on the power of Computer, and work inside Computer with all of your tools and files.
A teammate coordinates Computer sessions and other teammates to keep projects moving. They remember and learn as they work across different workstreams like marketing, sales, support, operations, or finance.
Ongoing project ownership
Teammates represent a new way of working with AI. Users can delegate ongoing actions to teammates so people can focus on outcomes rather than coordinating every task. Built on Perplexity’s focus on accuracy and Computer’s multi-model capabilities, teammates plan the work, check results along the way, and bring completed work back for review.
Teammates can investigate issues, research a market, or test improvements to a product, among other tasks. They remember project goals, task history, and shared files across runs. Each new task a teammate takes on builds on the work already done.
Proactive monitoring and follow-through
Teammates monitor ongoing work and follow up as things change. They investigate and act without waiting for a fresh query.
For example, a sales teammate notices when a regular customer stops transacting. The teammate reviews their order history and support issues and investigates what changed.
Then, it creates an offer relevant to that customer or flags any issues to resolve before reaching out. It shares progress updates and approval requests until it completes the work.
Teammates also remember past work and apply feedback to future tasks. If a user tells an operations teammate an agency needs two weeks’ notice, it factors that lead time into future project schedules.
Shared direction across teams
Teammates can work across teams. Add a teammate to a Slack channel and colleagues can hand it work or ask for updates on a task.
Teammates can also pass work to each other. One teammate finds bugs on a website and passes its findings along to another to prepare fixes.
Coordination across tools and tasks
Teammates build on the projects, skills, and memory already available in Computer. For example, a sales teammate can use a project’s existing account research and sales goals, follow a skill for writing outreach, and run a weekly automation to review the pipeline.
It brings those pieces together to identify stalled conversations, prepare follow-ups for review, and apply the results to the next week’s work.
Isolated environments and access controls
Teammates build on Computer’s existing tool and project permissions. Each teammate runs in a separate environment, with browser sessions separate from other teammates.
Saved credentials are encrypted and entered securely. Users can review completed work, take over the desktop, or redirect a teammate as it works.
Workflows across the business
Teammates handle ongoing work across business functions. These examples show how monitoring, investigation, and follow-through work together:
- Marketing: A marketing teammate manages social posts, email campaigns, ads, search engine optimisation, and review notes, creating new ads based on what’s working. It monitors campaign performance and competitors’ promotions, drafts fixes when results slip, and suggests responses when competitors change prices.
- Sales: A sales teammate finds opportunities in customer enquiries, past purchases, and unfinished conversations. It prepares outreach and quotes, follows up on replies, and flags support issues that need to be resolved before reaching out.
- Customer support: A customer support teammate reviews the previous day’s complaints, summarises trends, and flags cases that need a personal response from the CEO. It drafts those responses, follows up with internal teams on fixes, and tracks each case through resolution.
- Operations: A teammate keeps project deadlines, checklists, vendors, and paperwork on track. It follows up on missing items when a deadline is 72 hours away, helping teams address gaps before work falls behind.
Setup and availability
Teammates are initially launching on the web and soon on iOS for Perplexity Max subscribers. Free and Pro subscribers can upgrade in Settings > Account > Subscription.
To create and configure a teammate:
- Sign in to Perplexity on the web and select Teammates in the left navigation.
- Give the teammate a name that reflects the project you want it to do, then follow the setup steps.
- Connect the tools it needs. Add plugins such as Slack, GitHub, or Gmail. For GitHub, choose which repositories the teammate can access.
- Describe the work it should own. Include where the work comes from, what it should deliver, and when it should act.
- Assign it to a project and give it an initial task, such as researching a market, improving a sign-up flow, or investigating bugs.
We’ll be expanding teammates’ access and features in the coming weeks.
Try teammates today.

Pliny – Letters – Book 7 Letter 27 (On Ghosts)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
17:57:40 UTC
02:57:40 KST

BOOK SEVEN
LETTER 27
TO SURA
     
THE present recess from business affords you leisure to give, and me to receive, instruction. I am extremely desirous therefore to know your sentiments concerning spectres, whether you believe they actually exist and have their own proper shapes and a measure of divinity, or are only the false impressions of a terrified imagination?
     
What particularly inclines me to give credit to their existence, is a story a which I heard of Curtius Rufus. When he was in low circumstances and unknown in the world, he attended the newlymade governor of Africa into that province. One afternoon as he was walking in the public portico he was extremely daunted with the figure of a woman which appeared to him, of a size and beauty more than human. She told him she was the tutelar Genius that presided over Africa, and was come to inform him of the future events of his life:‹that he should go back to Rome, where he should hold office, and return to that province invested with the proconsular dignity, and there should die. Every circumstance of this prophecy was actually accomplished. It is said farther, that upon his arrival at Carthage, as he was coming out of the ship, the same figure accosted him upon the shore. It is certain, at least, that being seized with a fit of illness, though there were no symptoms in his case that led his attendants to despair, he instantly gave up all hope of recovery; judging, it should seem, of the truth of the future part of the prediction, by that which had already been furfilled; and of the misfortune which threatened him, by the success which he had experienecd.
     
TO this story, let me add another as remarkable as the former, but attended with circumctances of greater horror; which I will give you exactly as it was related to me. There was at Athens a large and spacious, but illreputed and pestilential house. In the dead of the night a noise, resembling the clashing of iron, was frequently heard, which, if you listened more attentively, sounded like the rattling of fetters; at first it seemed at a distance, but approached nearer by degrees; immediately afterward a phantom appeared in the form of an old man, extremely meagre and squalid, with a long beard and bristling hair; rattling the gyves on his feet and hands. The poor inhabitants consequently passed sleepless nights under the most dismal terrors imaginable. This, as it broke their rest, threw them into distempers, which, as their horrors of mind increased, proved in the end fatal to their lives. For even in the day time, though the spectre did not appear, yet the remembrance of it made such a strong impression on their imaginations that it still seemed before their eyes, and their terror remained when the cause of it was gone. By this means the house was at last deserted, as being judged by everybody to be absolutely uninhabitable; so that it was now entirely abandoned to the ghost. However, in hopes that some tenant might be found who was ignorant of this great calamity which attended it, a bill was put up, giving notice that it was either to be let or sold.
     
It happened that Athenodorus the philosopher came to Athens at this time, and reading the bill ascertained the price. The extraordinary cheapness raised his suspicion; nevertheless, when he heard tbe whole story, he was so far from being discouraged, that he was more strongly inclined to hire it, and, in short, actually did so. When it grew towards evening, he ordered a couch to be prepared for him in the forepart of the house, and after calling for a light, together with his pen and tablets, he directed all his people to retire within. But that his mind might not, for want of employment, be open to the vain terrors of imaginary noises and apparitions, he applied himself to writing with all his faculties. The first part of the night passed with usual silence, then began the clanking of iron fetters; however, he neither lifted up his eyes, nor laid down his pen, but closed his ears by concentrating his attention. The noise increased and advanced nearer, till it seemed at the door, and at last in the chamber. He looked round and saw the apparition exactly as it had been described to him: it stood before him, beckoning with the finger. Athenodorus made a sign with his hand that it should wait a little, and bent again to his writing, but the ghost rattling its chains over his head as he wrote, he looked round and saw it beckoning as before. Upon this he immediately took up his lamp and followed it. The ghost slowly stalked along, as if encumbered with its chains; and having turned into the courtyard of the house, suddenly vanished. Athenodorus being thus deserted, marked the spot with a handful of grass and leaves. The next day he went to the magistrates, and advised them to order that spot to be dug up. There they found bones commingled and intertwined with chains; for the body had mouldered away by long Iying in the ground, leaving them bare, and corroded by the fetters. Thc bones were collected, and buried at the public expense; and after the ghost was thus duly laid the house was haunted no more.
     
This story I believe upon the affirmation of others; I can myself affirm to others what I now relate. I have a freedman named Marcus, who has some tincture of letters. One night, his younger brother, who was sleeping in the same bed with him, saw, as he thought, somebody sitting on the couch, who put a pair of shears to his head, and actually cut off the hair from the very crown of it. When morning came, they found the boy's crown was shorn, and the hair lay scattered about on the floor. After a short interval, a similar occurrence gave credit to the former. A slaveboy of mine was sleeping amidst several others in their quarters, when two persons clad in white came in (as he tells the story) through the windows, cut off his hair as he lay, and withdrew the same way they entered. Daylight revealed that this boy too had been shorn, and that his hair was likewise spread about the room. Nothing remarkable followed, unless it were that I escaped prosecution; prosecuted I should have been, if Domitian (in whose reign these things happened) had lived longer. For an information lodged by Carus against me was found in his scrutore. Hence it may be conjectured, since it is customary for accused persons to let their hair grow, that this cutting of my servants' hair was a sign I should defeat the peril that hung over me.
     
I beg, then, you will apply learning to this question. It merits your prolonged and profound consideration; and I am not myself an unworthy recipient of your abounding knowledge. And though you should, after your manner, argue on both sides; yet I hope you will throw your weightiest reasons into one scale, lest you should dismiss me in suspense and uncertainty, whereas I consult you on purpose to determine my doubts. Farewell.

Repository navigation
Interactive installation and twelve-agent support
Run npx flawless-ui-ux@latest install, pnpm dlx flawless-ui-ux@latest install, or bunx flawless-ui-ux@latest install from your project. The terminal wizard lets you choose project/global scope, select agents, review destinations, and confirm before copying.

- Rendered inspection requires a separately prepared compatible Chromium and a running app URL.
- Context, inspect, and verify retain their existing behavior. The portable design guidance is unchanged by this release.
- Automated/runtime tests and recorded host inventories do not establish full WCAG conformance or matched model design-quality/latency outcomes. macOS terminal behavior remains unverified.

Just about anyone can rent access to White House IP addresses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
17:40:06 UTC
02:40:06 KST

Someone at the White House appears to be running software that could enable outsiders to rent access on the presidential network for just “a few dollars,” as reported by Krebs on Security and The Register. That’s according to findings from the security firms Layer3 Intel and Synthient, which discovered residential proxy activity on the White House network.
Just about anyone can rent access to White House IP addresses
Security researchers discovered residential proxy activity on the White House’s network.
A residential proxy opens up a way for people to rent access to a home IP address and route their internet traffic through it, allowing them to conceal where their activity is actually coming from. Some apps and browser extensions include third-party software development kits (SDKs) that put proxy nodes on a user’s device — whether users know it or not. Third-party services can then sell access to the residential proxies on users’ devices.
As noted by the cybersecurity firm Spur, people can legitimately use residential proxies for purposes like ad verification and quality assurance testing, but bad actors can also use them to bypass geolocation controls and defensive filters. Hackers have used residential proxies for all kinds of malicious activity, including to create botnets and carry out account takeovers.
At the White House, Layer3 Intel found that 28 residential proxy services routed traffic out of the network from October 5th to November 3rd. It notes that this activity typically happens between 5PM ET and midnight. “That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK,” Layer3 says. The SDK in question might be linked to the watch party app Rave, according to Synthient, which says the app “bundles 12 proxy SDKs into the platform.”
Synthient found “a number of Windows 10 and Windows 11 devices on the White House’s network beaconing to known proxy providers like Geonode, Infatica and Mellowtel.” As noted by Krebs on Security, Infatica is a proxy service founded by Vladimir Fomenko, the owner of King Servers, which was linked to 2016 cyberattacks on election systems in Illinois and Arizona.
Layer3 warns that the residential proxy is “public access,” adding that “anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it.”

Kobo will soon let you upload and sync your own ebooks across devices, for a price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
17:32:16 UTC
02:32:16 KST

Kobo is launching a new monthly subscription service called Stack that lets you upload your own ebooks and documents to the company’s servers where they’ll be synced across multiple devices and apps, including your reading progress, highlights, and annotations. Kobo Stack is similar to Amazon’s Send to Kindle feature that allows users to upload a wide variety of files to their Kindle libraries for free, but Kobo’s version will cost a few dollars each month.
Kobo will soon let you upload and sync your own ebooks across devices, for a price
Kobo Stack is a new monthly subscription service that’s first launching outside the US as part of a big e-reader update.
Kobo Stack is being introduced as part of a major 6.0 update to the company’s e-reader software, which is available in beta now as an optional upgrade ahead of a wider official release. Supported document types include EPUBs and PDFs up to 200MB in size and files can be pushed to Kobo Cloud using a drag and drop interface on the company’s website, or by emailing them to a custom address you get when you subscribe to Stack.
Your uploaded documents are synced and available anywhere you’re logged in to your Kobo account, including the iOS and Android apps, the Kobo website, and the company’s e-readers. Kobo Stack’s e-reader support is currently limited to recent devices including the Clara BW, Clara Colour, Libra Colour, and the Elipsa 2E, but access for older devices “made between 2018 and 2024 will arrive soon,” according to Kobo’s website.
The initial rollout of Kobo Stack is limited to Canada, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, the UK, and Spain, according to details Kobo CEO Michael Tamblyn shared on Threads, but not the US. Canadian pricing is $3.99 per month, while in the UK it’s £2.99 per month. Kobo is offering a free 90-day trial for those wanting to test it out, and there’s a 60-day grace period if you choose to cancel your subscription. That gives you around two months to download and back up any files you’ve uploaded, and to export your notes and annotations. After 60 days, everything will be permanently deleted.
Other features being introduced as part of the new Kobo firmware update include the ability to add multiple library cards so you can borrow books from several libraries through Libby, lower stylus latency on devices with pen support, improved accessibility with even larger font options, and support for EPUB files protected by LCP DRM.

Devvm.dev: One VM for every project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
17:30:22 UTC
02:30:22 KST

One VM for every project
An isolated sandbox with your project’s toolchain, ready for you or a coding agent to start coding.
Quick start
# Install devvm, and Lima with it
brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm
brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm
The install script in the Linux tab also works on macOS, and Installing lists its options.
1. Go to your project
Open a terminal and cd into any project folder.
2. Run devvm
devvm shows what the new VM gets. Confirm to make it, or customize it.
3. Start your agent
devvm opens a shell in the VM, whose prompt starts with (devvm), so start your agent there.
Claude Code needs your Claude login before its first start, which devvm agent login claude makes from the VM and keeps on your machine (your first VM). The next time you run devvm in the folder, it opens the same VM, and devvm tools adds an agent to a VM you already have.
What’s supported
Toolchains
devvm chooses the toolchains your project’s files call for, and you can choose more when you customize a new VM or name them with --tools (toolchains).
Coding agents
Claude Code, Codex and opencode run in the VM. Choose one when you customize a new VM, or choose them for every new VM in devvm setup (coding agents).
Layers
devvm ships the docker, nix and desktop layers, which you choose when you customize a new VM, and devvm layer new creates your own custom layers you can apply to any of your VMs (layers).
Why use devvm?
- Developers face attacks every day, such as supply chain attacks, leaked secrets, prompt injections and rogue agents.
- A sandbox limits the blast radius of an attack to what’s inside it.
- You know you should run your code and agents in a sandbox, but most tools need configuration and setup that’s hard to get right.
- devvm ships with sensible defaults so you can start coding in a sandbox with a single command.
Developer ready, zero config
- The base image comes with optional extras that you choose, such as oh-my-bash, fzf, zoxide (z), tree and tldr.
- Every VM gets your git name and email, so the commits made in it are authored by you or your agent.
- Ports forward on their own, so a dev server on :5173 in the VM opens at localhost:5173 on your machine (ports).
- devvm code opens the VM in VS Code over Remote-SSH (devvm code).
Isolated sandbox
- The VM mounts your project folder at the same path. Apart from your agents’ settings from devvm’s own store, which it gets read-only, it sees nothing else in your home folder (what a VM can reach).
- New VMs get the allowlist network tier by default, so they reach only an allowlist of hosts, through a proxy on your machine. You can choose a looser tier, internet or open, or a stricter one, none.
- On macOS, devvm locks .git’s hooks and config, so the VM can’t change what git runs on your machine (.git protection).
- With --clone, the VM works on a clone of the repo of its own instead of your folder, so nothing in it can touch your working tree or .git, and its work reaches your repo only when you fetch it.
- No sandbox closes every gap, so attack vectors lists what’s left open, and staying safe lists the habits that close most of it.
Ready in seconds
- The first VM builds a base image, and every later VM is a copy of it that starts in seconds (images).
- devvm builds each version of a toolchain once and shares it read-only, so all VMs use the same copy (shared tools).
Made for coding agents
- The agent runs in the VM, so an attack on it stays in the sandbox. It gets your settings, skills and MCP servers but never your history (coding agents).
- On every network tier, their secrets, such as your Claude Code token and your Codex login, stay on your machine, because the VM gets placeholders and devvm’s proxy puts the real ones into its requests on the way out.
Make it yours
- Your own layers are setup scripts that devvm builds into an image: devvm layer new mailpit starts one, and devvm --layers mailpit makes a VM with it (your own layers).
- devvm setup --layers gives every new VM the layers you choose, so your shell setup, aliases or dotfiles can go in a layer of your own that each VM gets unless you leave it out (extras of your own).
- --from starts the base image from a container image instead of Ubuntu’s, such as node:24 or your team’s own (starting from a container image).
- When the project has a devcontainer.json, devvm sets up its VM from the file’s container image, ports, environment and commands (devcontainer.json).
FAQ
What does it run on?
devvm runs on macOS and on Linux, on arm64 or x86_64. It needs Lima, which runs the VMs with Apple’s Virtualization framework on macOS and QEMU on Linux (backends). Homebrew installs Lima along with devvm, and on Linux, Lima also needs QEMU and access to /dev/kvm. Installing lists every requirement, and known limits lists what Linux hosts lack, such as .git protection.
Does the agent run on my machine?
No. You start the agent in the VM’s shell, so it runs in the VM, and you never install it on your machine. There it sees only what the VM can reach.
Is it free?
Yes. devvm is open source under the MIT license.
Start coding in a sandbox
Install devvm, then run devvm in any project folder.

Anthropic IPO valuation talks drop to $1.3T
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
17:21:15 UTC
02:21:15 KST

Anthropic IPO Valuation Talks Drop to $1.3 Trillion as Major Investors Balk at $1.5T Target
Anthropic's planned initial public offering — which could be the first for a frontier AI model developer — is being repriced in real time. Prospective investors are now discussing a valuation of $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion, down from the $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion range communicated to bankers just days earlier, and far below the $2 trillion figures floated in early October, Bloomberg reported Friday according to Investing.com [1]. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that three major prospective investors said the offering would need to be priced lower, with one suggesting a valuation closer to $1 trillion [1].
The reassessment follows Thursday's 6.4% plunge in the Nasdaq 100, which wiped out roughly $2.3 trillion in market value in its largest single-day decline on record [1]. The Cboe Volatility Index climbed to its highest level since April 2025 [1].
Valuation trajectory: $2T → $1.5T → $1.3T
Anthropic's valuation expectations have retreated in three steps. Early October discussions reached $2 trillion. After an investor briefing on financial performance, the range fell to $1.4–1.5 trillion. Thursday's market rout prompted the latest downward revision to $1.2–1.3 trillion [1]. Bloomberg's reporting suggests investors and bankers are still working toward an offering rather than abandoning the timetable [1].
Anthropic declined to comment on the valuation discussions [1][3].
Financials: explosive revenue, accounting-driven losses, massive compute commitments
The company's amended S-1 filing reveals the scale of both the opportunity and the capital intensity [2][6]:
- Revenue: $17 billion in Q3 2026, up 12× year-over-year. Nine-month revenue: $33.24 billion. Annualized run rate: ~$68 billion.
- Net loss: $23.3 billion in Q3; $104 billion for the first nine months. The filing shows 90% of the first-half loss ($72.4 billion of $80.5 billion) came from fair-value remeasurement of convertible notes — primarily from Amazon — whose carrying value rises as Anthropic's valuation climbs. This accounting effect largely disappears after the IPO when notes convert to equity [2].
- Operating performance: Roughly break-even in Q3 ($17.5B operating expenses vs. $17B revenue). Q2 showed ~$974 million operating profit. Operating cash flow was positive $3.9 billion in the first half; reports suggest free cash flow turned positive in Q3. Gross margin ~85% [2].
- Compute commitments: $895.4 billion in purchase and lease agreements, "substantially all" for compute and infrastructure. ~$447.5 billion due by end of 2030; ~$69.8 billion due in the 12 months after September 30, 2026 [2][6]. That near-term obligation is roughly four times current quarterly revenue.
The commitments explain why Anthropic needs to raise capital at scale. The IPO, led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley with 20 other banks, aims to raise at least as much as SpaceX's record $86.2 billion debut. The stock would trade on Nasdaq under ticker ANT [2].
METR finds 2× faster model improvement, driven by AI-assisted research
An independent evaluation by Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), given "unprecedented access to internal data" over roughly 11 weeks (mid-August through late October), estimated Anthropic is improving model capabilities on "well-specified tasks" around twice as fast as a year ago [4]. METR said it was able to "confidently" rule out compute growth as the driver, and said its guess was that the acceleration came from AI systems helping develop newer AI systems — the "closing the loop" dynamic Anthropic describes in its filing [4][6].
Caveats are significant. METR said the acceleration might be limited to tasks that can be graded automatically, not "messy" real-world tasks. It could also reflect understatement of prior progress. Internal disagreements and uncertainty among METR's team were noted [4]. Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment on the report [4].
CEO Dario Amodei publicly called for the industry to "slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models" in a September 12 essay, warning that recursive self-improvement could "outrun our ability to understand and control these systems" [4]. Amodei championed METR as an appropriate third-party evaluator; OpenAI's Sam Altman also supported the idea [4].
IPO timing uncertain: roadshow, October revenue, political headwinds
Reuters reported the roadshow was expected to kick off the week of November 9, with pricing the following week [3]. But four people familiar with investor discussions said potential investors are raising doubts about whether Anthropic can proceed on that timeline [3]. Investors are pushing for a more attractive valuation and are eagerly awaiting Anthropic's October revenue figure, which the company left blank in its updated S-1 [3].
A delay would amplify concerns about the AI ecosystem's health, particularly as ballot measures in multiple states limiting data center development have crystallized political opposition to AI infrastructure [3]. Microsoft tightened oversight of some data center projects from neocloud providers Nebius, IREN, and Nscale, Bloomberg reported Thursday; Nebius, Iren, and CoreWeave have each lost roughly half their value over the past month [3]. CoreWeave and SpaceX credit default swaps hit records implying rising default expectations [3].
Tech stocks have underperformed the S&P 500 by 10.7% over the past month — the most extreme one-month underperformance since May 2002, according to Truist Advisory Services [3]. Vanda Research said retail selling was the strongest since the COVID-19 pandemic [3].
What remains unknown
- Whether Anthropic proceeds at a $1.2–1.3T valuation, seeks a smaller raise, or delays past Thanksgiving.
- October revenue — a key data point investors are waiting for.
- How much of the $895.4B in commitments is firm versus contingent, and whether public-market investors will fund a capital plan that extends to 2045.
- Whether the "closing the loop" acceleration METR observed translates to broader capabilities or remains confined to benchmarkable tasks.
The distinction between a repricing and a postponement matters. If Anthropic goes public at a "more grounded valuation," it would test whether demand for leading AI businesses survives a sector correction [1]. For now, the company that says it wants to slow down is being forced to speed up its pitch to public markets.
Sources
- Anthropic IPO valuation discussions fall to $1.3 trillion ... (sg.finance.yahoo.com)
- Anthropic Q3 Results: $17 Billion Revenue, $23 Billion Loss ... (trendingtopics.eu)
- Exclusive-AI backlash could threaten Anthropic IPO timing ... (investing.com)
- Anthropic rapidly accelerating AI development amid slowdown calls, group says - ABC News (abcnews.com)
- https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/anthropic-ipo-valuation-discussions-fall-to-13-trillion-bloomberg-reports-5008125 (investing.com)
- https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026068676/anthropicpbc-sx1ax1.htm (sec.gov)

Notes on San Marino
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
17:12:05 UTC
02:12:05 KST

I spent three days in San Marino, a landlocked microstate completely surrounded by Italy. The people of San Marino are called the “Sammarinese.”
Travelling in Afghanistan is hard, but writing about Afghanistan is easy. If you are a white person in a place like Afghanistan, interesting things will happen to you. You don’t even have to do anything. Just stand on a street corner and strangers will stare at you and walk up to you and introduce themselves and shake your hand and offer you tea and food and show you around the city and you’ll find that it is harder to avoid getting into writing-worthy traveler adventures than to find them.
The European microstates of San Marino, Liechtenstein, Monaco, and Andorra have the opposite dynamic from a travel perspective. They are beautiful, wealthy, safe, lovely countries squarely rooted in one of the most beautiful, wealthy, safe, and lovely regions in the world. Hence, they are some of the most pleasantly boring/boringly pleasant countries in the world. Their populations are content, their governments are highly functional, their economies hum along, and nothing of note has happened in any of them since World War II.
So in a sense, travelling through these European microstates is the ultimate challenge of this blog. Not in the sense of paying that AK-wielding border guard $200 to let me out of Guinea was challenging, but in the sense that I needed to enhance my travel-writing focus to maximally mine pleasant dullness for anything interesting to write about.
I spent three days in San Marino, Liechtenstein, Monaco, and Andorra each, which, considering that they vary in geographic size from an American metro area to a large municipal park, and vary in population size from Bend, Oregon to Watertown, South Dakota, is a lot of time for each. I truly wanted to suck the travel marrow from these countries.
I’m not sure that I entirely succeeded and I’m not sure I’ll write about all of them, but first up is San Marino.
(Note – all images in this post can be expanded by clicking on them.)
Overview:
Population (2026) – 33,500 (5th lowest in the world)
Population Growth Rate (2025) – 0%
Size – 23.6 square miles/61.2 square kilometers (a little bigger than Manhattan)
GDP (nominal, 2025) – $2.25 billion (less than the estimated net worth of Mr. Beast)
GDP growth rate (2025) – 1.5%
GDP per capita nominal (2025) – $65,543 (comparable to Austria or Kentucky)
GDP per capita PPP (2023) – $78,000 (compare to about $59,000 for Italy, or $55-60K for the two adjacent Italian provinces)
Inflation rate (2021-2024) – 1.24-5.93% (Euro)
Biggest export – “Washing and Bottling Machines”
Median age (2025) – 48.6 years
Life expectancy (2025) – 86 years (ranked #2 in the world on some lists)
Murder rate (2025) – 0 per 100,000
Ethnicity – I don’t think there are any official records, but presumably mostly Sammarinese and Italian
Religion (2023) – 85-95% Catholic
Olympic Medals – 3 (1 silver, 2 bronze, all from the 2020 Tokyo Olympics)
Geography
Normally I don’t describe national geographic layouts in these posts, but I think it’s worth doing for the European Microstates to emphasize their tininess and respective geopolitical oddities.
San Marino is situated in a hilly/mountainous region in northern-central Italy, wedged between two Italian provinces (Rimini and Pesaro e Urbino). The nearest significant population center is Rimini (~150,000 inhabitants), a somewhat rundown coastal beach city with typically beautiful Italian old towns and cathedrals. It took two trains over five hours for me to get from Rome to Rimini, from which almost everyone enters San Marino.
The Rimini-San Marino bus runs every hour from morning to night, is surprisingly convenient, and takes about 45 minutes to drop off passengers in the heart of San Marino. Like every other European Microstate (except Andorra), there are no border checkpoints around San Marino.
While waiting for the bus at 10 AM on a Wednesday, two ambiguously accented European men approached me, one of whom was shirtless. I soon learned that they were Bulgarian BMW salesmen on holiday in Italy, and they decided to take a boozy day trip to San Marino. I never learned why the one guy was shirtless, including throughout the entire bus ride, but I guess Bulgarians are going to Bulgarian.
The capital of the nation of San Marino is the City of San Marino, which is situated in the center of the country. The City of San Marino is one of nine castelli (Italian for “castle”), their term for municipalities, or perhaps more accurately in this case, tiny provinces. Castello populations range from 11,200 to 1,000, and the capital is actually only the third-largest at a little over 4,000 inhabitants, largely due to the City of San Marino being given almost entirely over to tourist and government functions (in that order).
Having done almost no research on San Marino before arriving, my first surprise was how rural the country feels. I guess I implicitly assumed that microstates tend to be compact and urban, like Vatican City or Monaco, but most of San Marino feels vast and empty. It’s a land of fairly steep rolling hills with nearly all stores and homes built along primary avenues with few side roads.
Serravalle, the largest castello (holding about one-third of the population), is the relative exception and is the most urban part of the country, at least in a modern sense. It is based on the northern border closest to Rimini, so the San Marino Mall and accompanying wholesalers claim most of the commercial traffic coming from Italy. Many Sammarinese live in Serravalle to make daily commutes for work in Rimini:
Serravalle also has a bunch of middle-class European residential neighborhoods:
Once the bus from Rimini gets through Serravalle, tourists find themselves in remote European hill country…
Peppered with small Sammarinese towns…
Aside from the reasonably good infrastructure, the rest of the country doesn’t feel wealthy by European standards, but there is a quiet pleasantness to it. And in most of this pleasant, remote European hill country, you can see the City of San Marino in all of its glory built atop Monte Titano (the country’s highest peak), particularly the Three Towers, San Marino’s most famous sites:
But what is San Marino? Why is San Marino? How did a nation that is smaller than some data centers and can barely fill a large Chinese apartment block and is surrounded by a multi-time imperial power manage to survive as an independent sovereign state for arguably well over a millennium?
The Little Republic That Could
San Marino claims to be the world’s oldest continuously operating sovereign republic.
Its competition includes the Venetian Republic, which lasted 1,100 years from 697 AD to Napoleon’s conquest in 1797. Of other currently independent republics, Switzerland, or at least the Swiss Canton system, can arguably date back to the 1200s, but it was conquered and rearranged a few times, so it wasn’t continuous. If you want to really stretch definitions and claims, Iceland could argue that its current republican government began in 930 with the Althing (the world’s first parliament) with a few interruptions and long periods of sovereignty loss along the way.
But as far as I can tell, San Marino really is probably the longest-running independent republic in history, though even the most ardent Sammarinese fascist would admit that the nation’s official founding date of 301 is highly suspect.
The founding myth is that a Christian stonecutter named Marinus fled persecution in modern day Croatia to settle in remote central Italy where he could live a simple life of Christian tranquility. At the time, Christianity was a growing minority (maybe 10%) in the Roman Empire and faced periodic waves of persecution; official state tolerance of Christianity wouldn’t be enacted for another decade, and Christianity wouldn’t become the state religion until about 380. Meanwhile, Marinus’ home and church in central Italy became a small Christian community, which was later named “Saint Marinus” after its canonized founder, which was later Italianized into “San Marino.”
There is very little evidence of any of this happening. The story of Marinus is based on a Christian manuscript written at least 600 years later, and there is no evidence on the Church’s side of a canonization of any Marinus (though that isn’t too unusual for the time). The first good evidence of San Marino’s existence is the “Placito Feretrano,” an 885 AD legal ruling from the Church that affirmed the separation of the monastery of San Marino from the lands of the Bishop of Rimini. The document implied that the monastery had existed for some time, but San Marino was probably a part of the Kingdom of Italy, a realm ruled by a relative of Charlemagne. The earliest documented evidence of San Marino operating as an independent sovereign city state dates back to a notary deed from a land sale in 1243 that refers to two Consuls governing San Marino, which is the structure the country retains to this day (though the consuls are now called Captain Regents).
This is fascinating to me. As far as modern scholars are concerned, there was some sort of local political entity in San Marino created at some point in probably a 900-year time span (300-1243), but nobody knows when or how or why or who was involved. Even in the heart of Europe, only about 140 miles from Rome, it is possible for the history of an independent political entity to be lost to the sands of time. Of course, I know that the Dark Ages lost a lot of records and kept even fewer, but still, it sort of blows my mind that there is a contemporary European country and nobody knows how it started.
Records get much better from the 14th century onward. At that time, San Marino consisted of whatever community/monastery was on Mount Titano and a few surrounding towns. In the mid-15th century, San Marino joined a war on the side of Pope Pius II against the Lordship of Rimini and the Pope won; in 1463, for whatever contributions San Marino made, it was rewarded with enough Rimini land to double its size by annexing the Castelli of Fiorentino, Montegiardino, Serravalle, and Faetano, bringing the country to its maximum extent and the borders that it maintains as of 2026.
This era, around the 1300s and 1400s, was the height of political decentralization in Europe, at least post-Roman Empire, particularly in modern Germany and Italy. It’s actually pretty hard to recreate maps of the time, but Europe looked something like this:
But from that point onward, Europe went into a period of consolidation as bigger states ate or merged with smaller ones, including the prominent Italian city states like Venice, Florence, and Genoa, and the Papal States itself, all of which entered into the sort of hyper-competitive international diplomatic/warfare competition that produced Niccolo Machiavelli. The most fascinating part of San Marino’s history is that they managed to get through all the fighting and merging in one piece, let alone as an independent sovereign state.
So how did San Marino do it?
San Marino repeatedly made the right diplomatic deals, was in a unique geopolitical environment that catered to its strengths, was highly adaptable, and got very lucky.
IMO, if there was a secret sauce in the equation, it was paradoxically that San Marino was too meek to be conquered. It was a small, rural, isolated group of villages without any significant economic prospects, and it was intimately tied with its Christian monastery and Christian history. Conquest often wasn’t worth it for larger regional powers due to the reputational repercussions – marching an invading army into poor, little, pious, hyper-Christian San Marino in the heart of Italy was a bad look for stronger states. Later on, San Marino adapted diplomatically by emphasizing non-Christian elements of its culture and history, like its republicanism or conservatism, to similarly get on the right side of potential invaders.
I am going to try to go through the history of attempted and realized invasions/annexations of San Marino to give a sense of how this tiny state kept wiggling out of annexation. By my count, there are 13 such instances:
