The details are generally too technical to go into, but it basically amounts to San Marino being economically integrated into the EU in all but name, except for its immigration policy. And under this new agreement, San Marino has to ban compostable plastic forks, so there goes that joke.
Most of Italy’s economic policy-making regarding San Marino is offloaded onto the EU, but there are still separate Italy-San Marino agreements regarding standardized cross-border invoicing, social security contributions, corporate dividends, etc., most of which are pretty in-the-weeds and technical.
More interestingly, when it comes to tax differentials between San Marino and Italy, the microstate seems to be engaging in some minor arbitrage to its benefit. The following is an overview with many figures rounded or simplified because taxes are always needlessly insanely complicated:
So San Marino isn’t exactly a tax haven, but its tax regime is on the lower side of the EU and is better than Italy’s, particularly its income tax and lack of VAT.
But what about the canone doganale? Isn’t Italy supposed to be bribing San Marino to not leverage its sovereignty for tax arbitrage opportunities?
For much of San Marino’s history, the canone doganale made up about half of the San Marino government’s annual revenue, but today the annual payment is… €4.65 million. There is a decent chance that there are people reading this blog who have higher annual salaries.
The most recent canone doganale negotiation was signed in 1984 and set the annual rate at 9 billion Italian lire, where it has remained ever since. In 2025, the San Marino government’s total revenue was €718.55 million, making the canone doganale about 0.6%.
From what I can tell, the relative value of canone doganale payments declined because San Marino’s government modernized and began collecting sufficient tax revenue from conventional sources (ex. income taxes) and because San Marino is conservative enough and has good enough relations with Italy and the EU to not try any crazy hardcore tax haven stuff. As for why Italy keeps paying any annual canone doganale year-after-year, my best guess is that the sum is so small that no one cares enough to stop it.
I looked for studies or analyses that indicated that San Marino was profiting off regulatory/tax arbitrage, but I couldn’t find anything significant, at least nothing contemporary. In the early 2010s, after the 2008 Global Recession annihilated San Marino’s banking system, there were some IMF/EU reports that found Italian citizens avoiding Italian/EU banking rules and taxes by dumping their assets in San Marino, but the subsequent financial reforms pretty much ended all that.
My conclusion is that San Marino is barely, if at all, playing the microstate economic arbitrage game. Its citizens are a little wealthier than Italian citizens on average and pay a little lower taxes, but are mostly integrated into the wider Italian/EU marketplace. Interestingly, as of 2003, San Marino receives almost 9,000 workers from Italy daily, constituting 45% of private sector workers, while about 1,000 Sammarinese work in Italy.
Gun Stores
While walking around San Marino on my first day, I was surprised to find a conspicuous gun store (see above). Over the next few days, I saw a lot more of these stores, both in the touristy area at the capital and in the commercial area near the Rimini border. A quick look at Google Maps finds about 15-20 gun stores in the tiny Republic of San Marino.
What’s going on here? Is San Marino the low-key Texas of Europe when it comes to guns?
Nope, nothing that fun.
For one, the vast majority of guns sold in these stores aren’t lethal firearms, they’re airsoft guns, pellet guns, replica guns, blank-firing guns, decorative guns, and some tacticool accessories. From what I gather, San Marino has moderately looser real gun regulations than Italy and most other Western European countries, but it’s still quite strict by American standards.
Maybe the gun stores are a product of regulatory arbitrage? Perhaps San Marino allows the sale of more/better/stronger non-lethal guns than Italy?
This is slightly true – for instance, San Marino permits the sale of more powerful airsoft guns than Italy – but doesn’t have much explanatory power. The problem is that Italian law doesn’t allow Italians to purchase guns-that-are-illegal-in-Italy outside of Italy and then bring them back into Italy, so the regulatory difference doesn’t provide too much commercial benefit to the republic.
The boringer explanations for San Marino’s many gun stores are:
- Non-lethal guns are one of many commercial sectors that San Marino specializes in because it has lower sales/VAT taxes than Italy
- Some enterprising individuals set up the first gun store in the republic all the way back in 1965, and another enterprising local opened the first airsoft gun store back in 1990, before the hobby got big in Europe, so San Marino has a more developed local non-lethal gun industry than most European countries/cities
- It’s a novelty for European tourists who aren’t used to seeing gun stores
The Shinto Shrine
Nestled not too far off the main road in the north-center of San Marino is the San Marino Jinja, or Shinto shrine, along with a memorial for the March 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami, which killed almost 20,000 Japanese and caused the Fukushima nuclear powerplant disaster. The shrine was built in Japan after the earthquake, shipped to San Marino, and reassembled there. It’s a nice show of solidarity and support between two distant peoples, and the shrine itself is pretty cool:
But I couldn’t help but wonder why this thing was in San Marino. What does the tiny 35,000-citizen European Republic of San Marino have to do with the 120 million-citizen East Asian Japan?
Maybe the two countries have some sort of special economic relationship?
Nope. In 2012, San Marino exported €6.53 million worth of goods to Japan and imported about €2.4 million from Japan. Even for San Marino, that’s not a lot for its $2.25 billion economy.
Maybe there are a lot of immigrants/emigrants between Japan and San Marino?
Nope, not that either. According to public records, in 2024, there were seven Japanese nationals living in San Marino and four Sammarinese living in Japan.
So why does San Marino have a special Japanese shrine to commemorate a Japanese disaster, as opposed to an Indonesian memorial for its 2004 tsunami, or a Bangladeshi memorial for its 2009 Cyclone Aila, or a Nepali memorial for its 2015 earthquake, etc.
The answer is… a Sammarinese weaboo.
Even in the United States, the most important country on earth, most diplomats have very little to do. The ambassadors and diplomats assigned to China or Germany or comparably geopolitically important countries have a lot to do, and therefore such posts are highly coveted, but most U.S. ambassadorships have very little to do and are so unimportant that they are pawned off as spoils and political gifts. Like, the Ambassador to Belize from 2022 to 2025 was Michelle Kwan, an Olympic figure skater who had never been to Belize, has no Belize (or Caribbean) heritage, and knew nothing about Belize. Likewise, the Ambassador to Iceland from 2019 to 2021 was a Republican donor dermatologist who had never been to Iceland and had absolutely no political experience.
My speculation is that there are probably few people with less work to do in the world than the San Marino Ambassador to Japan, but San Marino happened to have one who took his role more seriously than anyone could or should expect.
When Manlio Cadelo was a young man studying in Paris, he became friends with a Japanese exchange student and was set on a path of Japanophilia. He attended the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, moved to Japan in 1975 to work as a journalist, began working at the San Marino consulate in Japan in the late 1980s, wrote two books about Japan (in Japanese), was appointed the official Ambassador to Japan in 2002, and was promoted to “Dean of the Diplomatic Corps in Japan” in 2011.
One might suspect that Cadelo capitalized on the 2011 earthquake and tsunami to manifest his love for Japan in physical form back home in San Marino by building a Shinto shrine, but that’s not entirely accurate. Plans for building a Shinto shrine in San Marino started all the way back in 2007; the 2011 disaster only seemed to accelerate the plans, particularly the funding, which came from the sale of “Japan–San Marino Friendship Charity Gold Coins.”
I know my tone is somewhat flippant, but I find this to be a cute story. The San Marino Jinja was the brainchild of a San Marino government diplomat, but it was built with private funding on private land with no input from the government or taxpayers of San Marino or Japan besides some time commitment from an unimportant diplomat. (The government of San Marino even put out a press release before the shrine was unveiled saying that it wasn’t involved in the project and didn’t spend a Euro on it.) A Sammarinese man with an unusual but apparently earnest and enormous love for Japan managed to bring a little piece of Nippon back to San Marino. Since its opening in 2014, it’s become an admittedly remote and rarely seen but cool part of San Marino’s tourism portfolio.
What Are These Weird Gambling Machines Everywhere in Europe?
On my first day in San Marino, I woke up at 5:30 AM due to jet lag, left my hostel at 6:30 AM to walk around, and stopped at 7:30 AM at a cafe for a cappuccino (X2) and some phone scrolling. At 8:30 AM, I noticed a lady who must have been in her 60s pounding espressos and pressing buttons on a machine in a dark, dusty corner of the room. I had seen these machines before across Europe, but there was something striking about this particular display of early morning degeneracy.
They’re called gaming machines or AWPs (Amusement with Prizes). They’re usually slot machines, but they can be card games or trivia or a few other varieties.
This is one of those things that I’ve been vaguely aware of because they pop up in British/Euro tv shows (the Inbetweeners and Peep Show come to mind) but they are uncanny to the American mind. Maybe something like this exists in the US in bars and cafes in Las Vegas or Reno, but otherwise, there is a (rapidly eroding) default blanket ban on gambling across most of the country. But in Europe, seemingly regardless of EU or national gambling laws, you can find these machines anywhere.
I don’t have a problem with these machines in general (though maybe little old retired Sammarinese ladies shouldn’t be using them at 8:30 AM on a Thursday); they’re just the millionth difference between American and European culture, and I want to know more about them. Are they a rite-of-passage for people? Do all young Europeans, particularly young boys, yearn to get a pint at the pub and take a run at the AWP? Are their odds horrifically rigged because drunk people are bad at probabilities? Do pubs need a license to have them because of gambling laws? Is there a reason a pub can’t have 50 of them and turn itself into a de facto casino? Are they locally made or is some Japanese pachinko conglomerate behind them?
San Marino’s Asymmetric Social Mach Bands (Or Does San Marino Conspicuously Display Its Sovereignty More Than Most Countries?)
In 2014, there was a Psychological Science paper called “Asymmetrical Social Mach Bands: Exaggeration of Social Identities on the More Esteemed Side of Group Borders.” Its thesis is that entities that are only marginally members of prestigious categories tend to emphasize their membership.
One of the examples they gave was airports – in the United States, small airports with international flights were more likely to have “international” in their names and reference their “international” nature on their websites than large international airports. Everyone knows that Washington D.C.’s Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport and New York City’s LaGuardia Airport are big enough to have international flights, so these airports don’t bother promoting that fact. But at first glance, no one would necessarily guess that Watertown International Airport in Hounsfield, New York would have international flights… but it is technically a legally designated “Airport of Entry” for private and military aircraft flying into the US, so it is “international” and promotes that fact in its name.
Based on this, I came up with a hypothesis – maybe European Microstates, compared to larger countries, display more promotions of the fact that they are indeed sovereign nations. Everyone knows that France and Germany are countries; not everyone knows that San Marino and Liechtenstein are. Conspicuous displays of sovereignty could include:
- Public national flags
- Public signage
- Memorials/monuments
- Naming conventions (not “Bob’s Petrol Station,” but “Andorra Petrol Station”)
In the case of San Marino, I would say that I saw slightly more references to the country’s independent sovereign nature within its borders than I did in typical Western European countries, like Italy or France. There weren’t too many Sammarinese flags in San Marino, but there were a lot of signs indicating national borders and a lot of stores/cafes/restaurants with “San Marino” in the title.
I’ll call this weak evidence in support of my thesis, but I’m hoping to see more conspicuous flag waving in Liechtenstein.
San Marino’s Negative “One Weird Tricks”
Try as I might, I can’t figure out who (some rationalist blogger?) came up with the one weird trick description for small, successful countries. The idea is that when it comes to national statistics, microstates or other small countries often tend to score at the top of positive metrics, and while these ranking placements say something about the quality of a country’s governance or people, we shouldn’t over-index on these stats because they tend to reflect strange quirks of these countries amplified by their small size that can’t be abstracted to general cultural/economic/governance recommendations.
For instance, San Marino has maybe the second highest life expectancy in the world at 86 years. Is this because the Sammarinese are the healthiest people on earth? Maybe, but it’s probably due to its population consisting almost entirely of longevity-prone Italians, but with higher levels of wealth, fewer immigrants (not counting Italians), and less crime compared to surrounding Italian regions.
San Marino also has the lowest childhood mortality rate on earth of 1.3 per 1,000, compared to 6.5 in the US, 3.9 in the EU (average), 2.7 in Italy, and 2.4 in Japan.
Or a more fun example – at the 2020 Tokyo Summer Olympics, San Marino won three medals, giving it a population per capita Olympic Medal winning rate of 88 medals per million people, by far the highest in the world. The US rate was only 0.335 medals per million people, and the China rate was 0.0623 medals per million people. Pathetic.
But what I’m really interested in is ways that trend is reversed. In which metrics are San Marino particularly terrible due to its microstate status?
The Sammarinese are like the eternals in Zardoz; great at living a long time but terrible at reproducing. With a 2024 birth rate of 4.2 per 1,000 residents, San Marino has the lowest birth rate on earth, beating out South Korea (4.7), Hong Kong (4.9), Ukraine (5.7), and Japan (5.7), and a European Union average of 7.9. It doesn’t help that the Sammarinese are quite old (median age of almost 50) and the young mostly migrate out of the country to Italian cities with better job prospects. Similarly, Italians may live a long time, but their birth rates are at the second-lowest in the European Union at 6.3, behind Spain (6.5), Greece (6.6), and Lithuania (6.6).
As of July 2026, San Marino is also dead last in the world in FIFA soccer international rankings at 211th place, losing out to Anguilla (a British territory), the British Virgin Islands (also a British territory), and the US Virgin Islands. The next worst sovereign nation is the Bahamas at 207th. I guess I can’t cast too much blame on a country of 33,500 mostly old people for doing badly in international soccer tournaments, especially when its closest comp of Liechtenstein is at 206th.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, at one point San Marino had the highest death and infection rate in Europe, beating out Belgium and Andorra in the two categories respectively. This is actually a little surprising to me; sure San Marino has a lot of old people, but it’s a mostly rural area and fairly geographically isolated.
But the most surprising to me of San Marino’s negative One Weird Tricks is how much it sucks at banking.
You typically think of tiny countries or Caribbean states as being very good at banking owing to being on the edge of international financial systems (though far less so these days). San Marino seemingly played this game decently well for decades and built up a large-for-its-tiny-size financial system (banking assets were more than 600% of GDP at peak) based mostly on wealthy Italian depositors dodging Italian/EU financial monitoring. But in 2008, the Italian government pressured San Marino to integrate into its financial system, which led to huge withdrawals and a decade-long slow-motion collapse of the Sammarinese banking system.
By 2020, San Marino’s four banks had a non-performing loan (NPL) rate of 63%, meaning that 63% of the value of the loans issued by these banks were not actively being repaid and would probably default. This is apocalyptically bad. At the time, right in the middle of the COVID-19 panic, the Italian rate was 4.1% and the EU rate was 2.6%. After the 2009 financial crisis, the US banking system’s NPL rate reached 5.4%. The Sammarinese government responded with bailouts, partial bank nationalization, and more reforms to avoid a complete collapse of the financial system, and it appears to have worked, bringing the NPL rate down to 53% in 2022, and 17% in 2025, which is still horrible, but not the-ATMs-don’t-work horrible.
Why is San Marino so bad at banking? Who the hell were they giving loans to?
My understanding as TLDR – San Marino’s position as a localized offshore Italian banking depository created a selection effect that attracted primarily Italian depositors and assets that were relatively underperforming; if they were performing well, they would stick to regular Italian and EU banks. In 2008, the international financial crisis hit and Italy cracked down on Sammarinese banking secrecy, both of which put tremendous strain on already substandard Italian assets, which backfired heavily on San Marino’s then-twelve banks. From 2009 to 2010 alone, Sammarinese banks lost 35% of their assets. Over much of the following decade, the banks failed to offload most of their bad assets while government regulators heavily intervened (even facilitating the consolidation of the country’s twelve banks into four), but the financial system still hit a breaking point in 2020 that was so bad that it required another massive bailout.
I don’t want to spoil the upcoming Notes on Liechtenstein, but I personally think San Marino should have, and still should, just dump tens of millions of euros on some Liechtensteiners to run their banking system.
The Empty Store Epidemic
In an earlier section, I described a chunk of San Marino as “an odd mixture of a bunch of light suburbs and strip malls built along winding hill highways” that gives the region “the feeling of roadside truck stops and strip malls.” This not particularly pleasant aesthetic is exacerbated by an apparent epidemic of empty or near-empty store fronts.
I am not the first person to notice this. I saw a few people mention it in Reddit comments and here’s a post on the r/liminalspaces subreddit about an eerie Sammarinese mall, which I also visited:
I’m not exactly sure why this is happening in San Marino. My first guess is that these empty/near-empty stores are a product of the aforementioned Sammarinese financial boom-bust cycle. From walking extensively around the country, I saw lots of commercial activity in the capital center with all the tourists, and near the Rimini border with all the Italian shoppers, but very little activity outside those zones. Most of the empty storefronts were outside these heavy-traffic zones, so maybe there was an attempt to expand San Marino’s commercial prospects, but the demand wasn’t great enough?
The Sammarinese Don’t Kill People… Unless Coke and/or Hookers are Involved
San Marino is an extremely safe country. From Googling and ChatGPT, I could only find seven recorded murders across the country’s history, occurring in 2002, 1973, 1853, 1854 (X2), and 1782 (a double murder).
But that’s not to say that the Sammarinese aren’t murdering people elsewhere.
In October 2002, San Marino citizen Enea Bruschi hit a Brazilian transwoman prostitute named Alessandra Sostenes Ferreira Fonseca with his car in Rimini, Italy, resulting in her death.
Bruschi claimed it was an accident, but the Italian police arrested him and charged him with murder. Normally, it’s difficult to prove murderous intent for vehicular homicide, but the police claimed Bruschi had gotten in an argument with Alessandra and then he ran her down with his car. As evidence, they pointed to numerous eyewitnesses, and Bruschi’s own testimony, where he admitted that he had finished work late, gotten drunk and high on coke at an Italian bar, started driving back home to San Marino, and then he accidentally hit Alessandra with his Renault 5 while looking away from the road because he was fiddling with the gear shift that had been acting up since a previous accident. Given these statements, the Italian police did not buy that Bruschi’s association with a trans Brazilian prostitute was merely in vehicular passing.
Further investigations did not bode well for Bruschi. For one, there was no problem with his car, except that the bumper had fallen off after he hit Alessandra. Worse, Alessandra’s roommate received three calls from her that night, two of which were recorded on voicemail, which presented Alessandra as being scared and running.
Given the number of news stories on this case, I guess this was the closest thing to the OJ Trial that San Marino has ever had; the legal saga extended for seven years on new charges and appeals. Bruschi was released shortly after his arrest for lack of motive evidence, then rearrested, then charged with murder, then convicted of negligent homicide (ie. manslaughter), then convicted of intentional homicide, then that was overturned, then the overturning was overturned, and finally, he was reconvicted of negligent homicide. At that point, the story is a bit hard to track, but he seemed to have served something like three or four years in prison, got released, started a beer company in San Marino, and then died mysteriously in 2019 at age 43.
The other relevant case is sketchier (from the prosecution side) and hard to find good info on because it happened in Cuba. In March 2003, four men, including San Marino citizen Gianfranco Ercolani, were charged with negligent homicide after the death of a 17 year old Cuban girl by cocaine overdose. One is left to imagine what these four gentlemen were doing with a coked up 17 year old girl. Though, surprisingly, she came from a prominent Cuban family, and so probably wasn’t a prostitute.
Ercolani’s story was that his Italian friend was for some reason hanging out with the 17 year old Cuban girl, and she ODed on coke, so the Italian brought her to Ercolani for help, and then Ercolani and his wife tried to take her to a hospital, but the legendary Cuban healthcare system wasn’t up to the task, and so she died. Ercolani tested negative for drugs.
In November 2005, after being detained in Cuba for over two years, Ercolani was convicted of negligent homicide and sentenced to eight years in a prison for foreigners. At some point, Ercolani briefly tried to flee Cuba by jumping on one of those refugee boats going to Florida, but he apparently chickened out. He was then rearrested, and the Cubans ended up throwing an extra year onto his sentence.
Fortunately for Ercolani, the San Marino diplomatic corps came to the rescue. Eventually. In August 2008, after spending about five years in Cuban detention and prisons, Ercolani was turned over to Sammarinese authorities to serve the remainder of his sentence in San Marino as its only alleged murderer. Once back home, Ercolani was soon put under a state of “semiliberty” where he could leave prison to go to work, and later, go to his house. There are probably worse ways to serve a manslaughter sentence.
Miscellaneous
- San Marino is the smallest country in the world by both geography and population to win an Olympic medal, an honor held by Liechtenstein until 2021.
- San Marino has a street named after Napoleon, “Via Napoleon Bonaparte.” This isn’t surprising given Napoleon’s historical interaction with San Marino and that there are dozens of streets in Europe named after Napoleon, plus a few more scattered ones around the world.
- What is more surprising is that San Marino has a street named after American President John F. Kennedy (“Viale John Fitzgerald Kennedy”) which is located quite close to the capital’s center. In September 1963, President Kennedy was kind enough to meet with a Sammarinese delegation in Washington DC, which was the first time a Sammarinese delegation had met with an American President in 44 years (President Wilson) and would be the last time such a meeting occurred for another 44 years (President Bush II). San Marino was so honored that when Kennedy was assassinated two months later, the republic named a street after him two days later.
- San Marino has its very own national dessert – the Torta Tre Monti, or “Three Mountain Cakes,” an allusion to its famous three towers. To be honest, I didn’t try one, because… they don’t look great. But I’m also not a fan of pistachio.

AI is the new dating dealbreaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
17:03:13 UTC
02:03:13 KST

When Irene moved to San Francisco last year, she started using dating apps as a way to meet new people, get to know her new city, and connect with others who care about the things she does. After the 25-year-old analyst downloaded Hinge and started swiping, she noticed a trend.
AI is the new dating dealbreaker
Swipe left if you’re not aligned.
AI is the new dating dealbreaker
Swipe left if you’re not aligned.
“Hinge has a prompt where you can say, ‘We’ll get along if”,” she recalls. “Sometimes people will be like, ‘Fuck AI.’”
Usually, the people who include this kind of value statement on their profile work in the arts, nursing, maybe graphic design. Within the span of a few minutes of sitting down and swiping, Irene shows me a second profile where this happened once more: “You should *not* go out with me if… you use AI.”
In San Francisco, the epicenter of tech, the metaphorical AI bomb went off in 2022 with the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT. Conversations surrounding artificial intelligence now permeate the dating scene in one shape or another. Over the past month, I bopped around the city, chatting with people at parties and coworking spaces and reviewing dating directories and other online profiles, trying to find out how AI affects the dating scene.
Responses varied wildly. For some, AI feelings take on a similar valence to traditionally political ones, showing up in dating profiles next to party affiliation or other signifiers, like the watermelon emoji symbolizing solidarity with Palestinians amid the war in Gaza. Others are wrestling with the ethics of dating someone who builds AI, considering the financial benefits a partner in the industry can bring, weighing whether to have children in a future this uncertain, or even handing their love lives over to it entirely.
On a street near Berkeley, I meet up with Kyle. (His name has been changed so that he can talk openly about his personal life.) Kyle is a researcher at an AI safety nonprofit initiative, and although he is just in his early 20s, he’s already thinking about death. In the AI safety community, some experts see a 10 percent chance of humans going extinct due to AI taking over. This apocalyptic possibility is always top of mind when he navigates conversations with a potential partner: The rapid development of AI shapes how he thinks about whether he wants to have kids or where he might live long term — if there is even a long term.
“It’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future.”
“A lot of people are planning for what they want their life to look like five, 10, 15 years down the line,” Kyle says, raising his gaze and looking off into the distance. Life could change depending on whether the world manages to get AI alignment right, he tells me. “For me, it’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future,” he says. He tries to have these conversations in person rather than over text, so a date can ask follow-up questions about why he sees the future the way he does.
For now, he’s focusing on finding a partner with whom he enjoys spending time.
When I ask Kyle if he would date someone who works in artificial intelligence or tech, he says that he would have to think hard about it. He believes that a lot of people who work at frontier AI companies are doing things that he considers pretty heinous. “They don’t think very hard about the societal impacts of their actions because they’re mostly in it for the paycheck or because it’s interesting,” he says.
But Bryan, who works at a frontier AI company and also asked to go by a pseudonym, doesn’t believe that feelings about AI matter when it comes to romance.
“I just don’t think it’s a factor at all. Like, it’s the least [relevant] thing,” says Bryan, who recently started a relationship. To him, dating is more about weighing a series of factors: how someone talks and approaches problems, how they have fun. Despite his day job (and whatever someone like Kyle might think of him for it), he believes that working out more and looking better probably increases someone’s chances of getting a match way more than any AI or non-AI affiliation. But, he says, “The one way it interacts is that there are a bunch of people who are rich from AI, and, you know, being wealthy is always a plus.”
Bryan isn’t exactly wrong about the benefits of a high-paying job in AI. With the IPOs of Anthropic and OpenAI in the next year, matchmakers have found that clients are specifying “AI engineer” on their list of preferred dating profile qualifications. And stability is particularly attractive right now: According to a CBRE report released in August, more than 20,000 AI jobs were added to the San Francisco Bay Area’s technology workforce, even as overall tech talent contracted by 6 percent since 2022. “Member of technical staff” roles have become very lucrative jobs; the average salary of an AI researcher can be around $300,000. According to the New York Post, one matchmaker found that her client booked a six-month stay in San Francisco because of the possibility of meeting a significant other who might be connected to an AI company going through an IPO.
AI is reflected in the way the technology is seeping into San Franciscans’ everyday habits — including those that shape relationships, from how people process their feelings to whom they confide in.
Andromeda, who works as an EMT and a registered behavior technician as well as an AI security analyst, says she’s worried about the unintended consequences of talking to AI chatbots, especially for questions about (and possibly the replacement of) human connection. According to a study released by Elon University, 27 percent of Americans are turning to AI chatbots with personal, emotional, or social queries. Thirty-eight percent of the surveyed group said they occasionally tell AI things that they would not tell other people, including their romantic partners. Andromeda weighs the pros and cons of dating someone who would use bots for “emotional regulation.”
“Socially and psychologically, it’s a big deal, and we have to talk about it,” she says. She appreciates the role that a chatbot can play to help someone better express themselves. “I would certainly date a man who uses AI to talk through intense thoughts and feelings and to brainstorm clarity.”
At the same time, she is also reluctant to date someone who might abuse a chatbot, since it’s maladaptive behavior and does not represent good values for model welfare. “If they treat ChatGPT badly today, it will be me tomorrow!”
“There are a bunch of people who are rich from AI, and, you know, being wealthy is always a plus.”
If Andromeda worries about what people tell chatbots, others have gone a step further and let AI do the talking for them.
At the Hugging Face Open Source Week party, Joseph, a 21-year-old software engineer, explains how he has automated his dating life. Working 14 hours a day to launch his startup, he has decided to outsource swiping on Hinge entirely to an AI agent. The agent is managed by his human virtual assistant from the Philippines and has been fine-tuned to mimic the way that he speaks and acts. Looking at each profile, the AI agent sends tailored outreach messages to spark a conversation. After some back and forth, the agent determines if the woman is compatible with Joseph and, if so, books open slots on his weekend calendars for dating in person.
“If you are a founder, you have to put a value on your time, so you can’t be doing low-leverage activities. Protect your dopamine, folks,” Joseph tells me at The Midway in San Francisco’s Dogpatch district, where hundreds don white bucket hats and dance next to Hugging Face’s round, foam emoji mascot. “It’s kind of a copy-and-paste sequence that happens with every girl to get to know about you, understand your backstory, and so on and so forth.”
He’s not alone. A 2025 survey by Match and the Kinsey Institute found that 26 percent of singles in the United States use AI tools to enhance their dating experiences. Hinge now has an AI tool to generate suggested responses and Bumble, which will soon phase out swiping, has launched Bee, an AI assistant-facilitated matchmaking tool. (Bumble VP of Communications Natalie Logan said in an email that Bumble has not yet announced the update to the swipe, and that Bee operates independently of that update.)
“It has been extremely successful. I’m averaging two closed conversions a week,” he says, meaning that he goes on two dates with two different people. The women on the other side don’t know. The point is to meet in real life. The overall process has lowered what he calls “CPN,” or “cost per nut.”
At 29 years old, JJ has stopped using dating apps. Instead, she turns to the Date-Me Directory — a collection of longform, resume-like documents where people write personal dating profiles — to find a partner. Two years ago, she worked in product design in New York, but she transitioned into the AI safety field because she felt that it aligned more with her effective altruist morals.
Upon reviewing troves of Date-Me Docs for the San Francisco / Berkeley area, I noticed that quite a few people mention “the singularity” as a factor of whether to have kids. The so-called “singularity” is the point of when technology overtakes human control; some have pointed to the development of true artificial general intelligence as the point of no return. According to JJ, many people in AI safety specifically use the Date-Me Docs as a way to meet people.
“Don’t want kids in the pre-singularity future, if there’s a post-singularity future then I might want kids then,” one document states.
On the other hand, similar to climate doom anxieties, other people are looking at whether having children is ethical amid massive structural changes in society caused by AI.
“Is the world good, getting to a good place, or is it bad? And if it’s good, baby. If not, no baby, because you’re gonna bring a baby into a world full of potential suffering,” JJ says, explaining the train of thought that these Date-Me Doc potential suitors might have. She does not consider herself a doomer, but she is still pressed for her own singularity timeline. (2029, she suspects.) If anything, she jokes that the approaching end times makes her more likely to want a baby around: “If the bomb gets me, I want to be holding a shiny child.”
These existential concerns have translated into a backlash against tech, San Francisco included. “Stop the AI” rallies have spread to events like Salesforce’s Dreamforce convention and OpenAI’s DevDay, with protestors calling out tech companies and their roles in data center development and ICE raids.
“If there’s a post-singularity future then I might want kids then.”
That skepticism has spilled into how people size up a potential match, even at local events designed to bring the Bay Area together. At a pop-up “Date My Friend” pitch event at the Kilowatt Bar in the Mission District on a Saturday evening, a dozen people pitched their friends and exes to a crowd of more than a hundred.
“He works in tech, but he’s unhappy about it,” one person announced to a chorus of cheers. Other people cracked jokes that their PowerPoints were clearly made by humans, not AI.
Annalise Wulf, 26, one of the three cofounders of the “Date My Friend” series, says that although people in San Francisco try to “tech maxx” their lives, more tech workers with crazy schedules are interested in analog, in-person events to go back to the roots of meeting and creating community. “It’s like, ‘I’m here because I’m not using an AI dating app right now. Like I’m trying to do something different,’” Wulf says.
“I do think it’s maybe popular now to be more anti-tech,” says Lucy Segraves, 28, one of the other cofounders. If someone is working for a company that people see as perpetuating war crimes through their technology, she might be more hesitant to date them.
But ultimately, she says, there are more immediate concerns. “As a person with a non-tech job, I never judge someone if they do work in tech,” Lucy says. “Because that’s unfortunately where the money is, and we’re all just trying to make it in life.”

GPU-Accelerated Weight Teleportation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:49:00 UTC
01:49:00 KST

Introduction#
Large-scale RL is different from either large-scale pretraining or large-scale inference. A key difference is that the training weights and the sampler weights should ideally match as closely as possible, which requires the trainers sending weight updates to the samplers. This creates a bottleneck: one must either use high speed intra-cluster networking to send weight updates or accept the often-meaningful delay that comes with attempting to communicate terabytes of model weights, not to mention blocking on the samplers. We introduce a faster weight update paradigm, in most cases allowing better-than-intra-cluster speeds, regardless of whether the samplers and trainers are co-located within the same cluster.
The design starts from the widely adopted idea of delta weight sync1Miles v0.1: Production-Level Post-Training, §4.3 Disk-Delta Updates.. We co-designed an entire Blackwell-native compression/decompression pipeline combining the following techniques:
- Massively parallel GPU compression, with distributed ownership and fault tolerance.
- A curated double compression algorithm with heterogeneous CPU-GPU decompression.
- Blackwell Decompression Engine (DE) and hardware-native decompression algorithms, fully overlapping DE with ordinary GPU compute.
- Tiny memory buffer overheads across trainers and samplers, CPUs and GPUs.
As a result, we bring the sampler pause time below 0.23 s and the end-to-end weight sync time below 4 s in our Ampersand production RL configuration, fully saturating the Blackwell Decompression Engine pipeline and making the decompression ASIC the bottleneck for sampler pause time. The implementation is so fast in terms of both end-to-end weight sync time and sampler pause time that even intra-cluster P2P RDMA is slower for most real-world workloads.
For the rest of this article, we use the following as a consistent workload proxy. The model is NVFP4 GLM-5.3, with 445 GB of canonical weight tensors. RL training signals are sparse, with only a tiny portion of weights being updated during each training step, so we mutate 0.085% of the checkpoint as a proxy for one steady-state update. The trainer has 8 nodes with 64 B300 GPUs. Each rollout receiver has two TP4 NVFP4 GLM-5.3 engines on one 8-GPU B300 node. The diagrams use fewer GPUs and model layers for clarity.
CPU disk delta weight sync#
To explain our design progression, we need to understand the foundations of delta weight sync and why a naive implementation is not enough.
Delta update algebra#
# trainer
mask            = weights_old ⊕ weights_new
# rollout
weights_updated = weights_old ⊕ mask
                = weights_new
The core of delta weight sync is the bitwise XOR (⊕) operation. Before a training step, the rollout engines and trainer hold identical weights. The trainer finishes a training step and advances from weights_old to weights_new. The trainer performs a bitwise XOR between weights_old and weights_new to obtain a mask with exactly the same shape as the weights. The 1s in the mask indicate that the weight bit at that location has flipped, and 0s mean unchanged. The rollout engines need weights_new to sample from the new policy for the next RL step. To obtain them, the engines only need to flip the same weight bits. Thus, we transfer the mask to the rollout engines and apply bitwise XOR between their weights_old and the mask. Since the weights are viewed as a long contiguous sequence of bits, their specific data types do not matter and floating-point arithmetic or rounding is not involved.
But masks have the same size as the weights, so directly transferring masks does not save anything versus transferring the full weights. What truly makes the delta sync approach attractive is the following insight. In RL, training signals are sparse, so only a tiny portion of weights are updated during each training step. That means the masks contain mostly 0s and only a tiny portion of 1s. A lossless compression algorithm can then compress the masks into a tiny transfer payload.
Model checkpoint as a handoff#
Now let’s look at a naive but clean delta weight sync design within the RL loop. The trainer and rollout engines need to sync their checkpoints, so let’s use model checkpoints as the handoff. The trainer performs a training step, computes the mask, compresses it into a small payload, and sends the compressed mask to the rollout engines. The rollout engines load and decompress the mask, patch the checkpoint to match the new trainer weights, and reload weights from that checkpoint. Since the checkpoint is the handoff, the rollout engines reuse the same code path as server startup. We don’t need to handle how the rollout engines re-shard or map the weights.
The existing disk-delta implementation in Miles1Miles v0.1: Production-Level Post-Training, §4.3 Disk-Delta Updates. largely follows this design:
From the measurement above, the compressed payload is only 0.876 GB, matching our expectations. However, this benefit has been completely offset by other significant overheads:
- Trainer compression adds latency.
- Checkpoint patching requires a disk round trip.
- Rollout engines need to reload the entire checkpoint from disk.
GPU accelerated (de)compression#
The RL stack already runs on distributed GPU clusters, so the intuitive next step is to make this pipeline GPU-accelerated, using their powerful parallel compute and high-bandwidth HBM.
A strong baseline with Blackwell-native DE#
Blackwell has a fixed-function Decompression Engine (DE) 2Decompression Engine FAQ. that performs certain supported decompression algorithms extremely efficiently. To make our baseline sufficiently strong, we directly codesign the GPU-accelerated pipeline with GPU-native (de)compression algorithms and Blackwell-native dedicated hardware.
The table below compares (de)compression algorithms on GPUs3NVIDIA nvCOMP Quick Decision Matrix, qualitative ratings.:
Table 1. GPU codec trade-offs and Decompression Engine support.
As shown in Fig. 4 above, the major overheads are on the receiver side, including decompression, checkpoint patching, and engine reload. Therefore, we prioritize receiver-side decompression performance, starting with LZ4/Snappy for a fast GPU codec pipeline.
LZ4 and Snappy are from the same algorithm family 4LZ4 and Snappy are byte-oriented LZ77 codecs: both encode literals and backward copies, without an entropy-coding stage. See the Snappy format and LZ4 block format., with one noticeable difference in how the copy commands are encoded. A single Snappy copy command can cover at most 64 bytes. LZ4, however, can encode a much longer region directly with fewer copy commands. Because the RL update masks are mostly filled with long sequences of zeros, LZ4 tends to compress the final payloads more compactly than Snappy. Note that the exact results can be implementation specific. Our experimental results support this intuition. On the same proxy mask, nvCOMP LZ4 compressed more compactly than Snappy. The LZ4 baseline produces a complete publication of 5.36 GB. Therefore, we choose LZ4 as the codec for this design.
Since we have decided to use GPUs for decompression, the decompressed masks are already resident in GPU HBM, and paying for a disk round trip for checkpoint patching does not make sense. Therefore, we implemented Triton kernels to apply the bitwise XOR in place in GPU HBM. The tiling and address mapping between model layers and decompressed masks can be complicated, so we prepare this metadata on the CPU and let the Triton kernel read from the prepared plan. As a result, the XOR application stage can be done extremely efficiently by a single Triton kernel launch for the entire model.
On the trainer side, we employ all the existing GPUs used by distributed training to compress the masks in parallel. Distributed training already means distributed tensor ownership, but it may still duplicate some model weights, especially with context parallelism (CP) and data parallelism (DP). For compression, we remap weight ownership so that the GPU ranks collectively cover the entire model checkpoint exactly once, with each rank owning only a subset of the weights it holds for distributed training. This has three major advantages:
- Compression is greatly accelerated by parallelizing it across the existing training GPUs.
- Weight-gathering traffic is greatly reduced because we only need to gather rank-local compressed payloads instead of the original model weights.
- The memory pressure from holding earlier versions of the weights is greatly mitigated across all the existing ranks.
Putting the design together: all trainer GPUs compress concurrently, rollout GPUs decompress LZ4 directly using DE, and a single Triton kernel launch updates all model weights in HBM. All weight-sync network traffic carries compressed payloads, and disk checkpoints are completely out of the hot path. This is already an extremely strong baseline: for the same proxy payload, trainer-side preparation and compression take 0.834 s, and receiver-side work takes 6.041 s.
Working with low-precision RL#
Since compression, decompression, and bitwise XOR all treat model weights as a contiguous buffer of bits, delta weight sync works losslessly with low-precision RL.
Low-precision weights can even absorb small high-precision updates, such as changes to low mantissa bits, making the delta payload even smaller.
An interesting detail is how to work with high-performance MoE kernels like the one we described in Faster-than-light NVFP4 decode—with precision. To achieve aggressive fusion, high-performance kernels may reorder the logical weights into a different physical layout. See the example below of pairing gate and up weights in groups of 64. Using model checkpoints as handoffs dodged this complexity earlier, but we have to solve it when we want to update the weights in place.
Since the decompressed masks have the same shapes as the model weights, we can remap the masks the exact same way so they become pointwise aligned with the remapped model weights again. This adds another layer of complexity to the tiling and address mapping between model layers and decompressed masks, but all of this metadata is prepared on the CPU. The Triton kernel for XOR application only needs to read the prepared plan.
The remaining trade-offs#
We already have an extremely strong baseline: for the same proxy payload, trainer-side preparation and compression take 0.834 s, and receiver-side work takes 6.041 s. However, two critical flaws remain:
- Payload size. On the same proxy workload, the nvCOMP LZ4 payload size is 5.36 GB, while the CPU Zstd baseline is only 0.876 GB, so LZ4 transfers 6.1x as many bytes. GPU-friendly compression algorithms do not necessarily optimize for a high compression ratio. According to Table 1, there is no single compression algorithm that combines a high compression ratio, fast decompression, and DE support.
- GPU buffer size. GPU decompression also means GPU input and output buffers. To fit the large decompressed masks in HBM, we must evict the KV cache. First, this complicates memory lifetime management. More importantly, evicting the KV cache effectively makes overlapping rollout decoding with decompression impossible, since the KV cache is gone.
From accelerator to teleporter#
We now show how to turn GPUs from accelerators into teleporters, reducing the rollout pause for weight sync to under 0.23 s.
Double compression with heterogeneous decompression#
Compressed payloads can still contain repetition, especially with GPU-friendly algorithms that do not necessarily optimize for compression ratio. We therefore consider adding a round of Zstd compression on top of GPU-friendly codecs such as LZ4 or Snappy:
Table 2. Payload sizes before and after outer Zstd compression.
Empirically, Snappy + Zstd produces a meaningful reduction in payload size compared with the LZ4 baseline. Adding Zstd to LZ4, however, provides a smaller improvement. One possible explanation is that Snappy’s simpler copy commands are easier for Zstd to compress, even though Snappy is less efficient than LZ4 at encoding long runs of zeros in a single pass.
Double (de)compression unlocks receiver-side design opportunities beyond reducing payload size. Since the outer Zstd stage operates on small, already compressed payloads, the CPU can handle this decompression efficiently without using GPU compute or HBM. Rollout decoding can continue normally while the CPU receives the delta update payload, prepares metadata, performs the outer decompression, and stages the resulting Snappy payload in pinned CPU RAM buffers for the GPUs to consume later.
DE can directly consume pinned CPU RAM and output to GPU HBM5CUDA Driver API cuMemCreate, using CU_MEM_LOCATION_TYPE_HOST_NUMA and CU_MEM_CREATE_USAGE_HW_DECOMPRESS in allocFlags.usage. Ordinary pinned allocations are not sufficient; see NVIDIA’s DE memory requirements., which fits seamlessly into this CPU-GPU decompression pipeline. This also eliminates the need for input staging buffers in HBM, slightly reducing GPU memory pressure. We also found empirically that this approach achieves higher host-device transfer bandwidth than our own ring-buffer implementation.
Overlapping DE and SM#
To fully saturate DE, we use one final feature. Since DE is a fixed-function hardware block for decompression, its work can overlap with GPU compute on the streaming multiprocessors (SMs). For our use case, this means overlapping DE decompression with the Triton bitwise XOR kernel on the SMs. We designed a double-buffered software pipeline in which DE decompresses into one slot while the SMs read from the other. We stream all model weights through these buffers, layer by layer:
As the Nsight Systems profiling trace above shows, the DE pipeline is fully saturated, and Triton kernels are completely hidden by the DE setup-decompression loop, bringing the pause below 0.23 s.
This double-buffered streaming design also eliminates the need for a decompression output buffer for the full model. The two buffers only need to hold two model layers at a time, so they fit within the GPU memory outside the KV cache, typically reserved for activations during inference. No KV cache eviction or changes to the inference engine’s GPU memory pool are needed.
Assembling the weight teleporter#
Now it is time to assemble the complete GPU weight teleporter in our RL stack:
Since Snappy is a more GPU-friendly compression algorithm, the combined trainer-side preparation and compression time falls from 0.834 s with LZ4 to 0.789 s, even with an extra round of Zstd compression. The rollout engines take 2.355 s to pull the payload, prepare metadata, decompress the outer Zstd layer, and stage the Snappy payload. Rollout inference can continue normally because preparation uses neither GPU compute nor GPU memory. Only DE-SM streaming blocks inference, for just 219.6 ms.
Beyond the steady-state RL loop#
So far, we have mainly focused on steady-state trainer-rollout weight updates, the core RL hot path. However, this approach also provides general-purpose infrastructure for other use cases:
Eval, fault tolerance, and resuming from trained checkpoints#
Unlike steady-state trainer-rollout weight updates, where the version always increments by one, several use cases in the RL loop require updating from different weight versions:
Table 3. Base versions for evaluation, recovery, and resumed training.
These use cases require maintaining deltas against at least two additional versions: the last eval version and the rollout/eval engines’ base version. Due to our fully distributed ownership design on the trainer side, the weights are sharded and distributed across the entire training engine. Each CPU only needs to hold the extra versions of its assigned shards, without adding significant memory overhead. Also, the processing for these auxiliary deltas can be easily overlapped with the payload transmission or preparation phase on the trainer-rollout hot path, without lengthening the rollout pause, which remains below 0.23 s.
Another important detail about resuming from a trained checkpoint is that the resumed checkpoint may have advanced many steps beyond the base version and accumulated a decent amount of delta. How do we make sure the rollout engines still have enough memory buffers for staging the larger delta? The LZ4 + Zstd codec we previously did not adopt becomes a good fit here. It has a larger final payload size, but the startup transfer only happens once and can overlap with other startup work. The smaller inner payload size helps to keep the staging buffer small even with a larger accumulated delta. The trainer-rollout hot path can still use the Snappy + Zstd codec to benefit from the small final payload size.
Inference deployment and beyond#
This infrastructure also greatly simplifies inference serving and deployment. Whenever a new trained checkpoint comes out, we only need to send its tiny compressed delta across data centers instead of a full model checkpoint. The inference engine launches from a base checkpoint and simply makes a single call to /update_weights_from_gpu_delta to pull and apply the latest delta. To release resources that are no longer needed in a pure inference use case, we have implemented an opt-in release_state argument that will automatically clear any staging buffers, GPU kernels, and CPU threads related to delta updates after the delta is applied.
We also treat this infrastructure as a superior alternative to LoRA adapters to some extent. Our approach compresses full-parameter deltas into tiny final payloads, while LoRA keeps the payload small by limiting the ranks of the updates. What’s more, our approach can swap different deltas on and off during serving with just one API call and a pause of less than 0.23 s, completely imperceptible to end users.
Speeding up research iterations#
Together, these capabilities let us iterate on research experiments much more rapidly. During each training checkpoint export step, we always export the auxiliary compressed delta against the base version and save it to disk. We can immediately move it across data centers and conduct experiments without waiting for checkpoint conversion or inter-cluster checkpoint transfer. The inference endpoints can immediately pull the refreshed delta on the fly with just one API call and do not need to restart.
We have also removed a major source of network traffic both between clusters and within our cluster. As a small bonus, this also helps relieve network congestion and improve stability.
Open source#
We have open-sourced the implementation across the stack:
- Orchestration, distributed GPU compression, fault tolerance, and delta checkpointing in Miles6Miles GPU-delta publication and receiver coordination..
- The heterogeneous decompression pipeline with full DE-SM overlap, optimized Triton kernels, and the one-shot /update_weights_from_gpu_delta API in SGLang7SGLang GPU-delta decompression and in-place weight updates..
This effort uses nvCOMP heavily. We thank the NVIDIA nvCOMP team for their high-performance implementations of compression and decompression algorithms.
Conclusion#
We do not foresee further work on RL weight sync because we believe this is the optimal solution for existing hardware. The rollout pause time is so short, the CPU/GPU memory footprint is so small, and the support for fault tolerance is so complete that even the best intra-cluster P2P RDMA implementation becomes obsolete. We have used one of the fastest GPU-native codecs, fully saturated the DE pipeline, and overlapped SM work; the bottleneck for weight sync has become hardware throughput.

How Akai and Moog are embracing vibe-coded mods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:34:39 UTC
01:34:39 KST

inMusic, the parent company of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more, has decided to embrace the modding community. In an interview with The Verge, inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell said, “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want.” That “toolbox” includes making the code for devices like the recently teased MPC Sample Key open source, but also offering developers an SDK to make modifications easier and lessen the risk of bricking your beloved sampler.
How Akai and Moog are embracing vibe-coded mods
inMusic is making open-source MPCs, hackable synths, and mod-friendly DJ decks.
While Akai is eager to see what the modding community cooks up, and has started seeding devices to developers ahead of the official release of the Sample Key, the company takes reliability seriously. O’Donnell said the company wants to “make sure that our official software is completely stable and good for an artist on stage.” He can’t have Fred Again going on stage and discovering his MPC is riddled with bugs. But he also wants people to feel comfortable tinkering. “We’ll try to give them a reset button,” he said so “They can experiment with it, and then not lose what they have.”
The company is planning to make a big splash NAMM, the annual convention of music manufacturers in Anaheim, with Creator Lab, where it will let technically curious musicians get some hands-on time hacking 22 new products from across its brands. That includes products from Moog, that might not seem like a natural pairing for vibe coding because of its analog design. But O’Donnell thinks it can be, “if we open it up correctly.” That will involve building a platform for devs to work around the analog parts of the circuit.
Other companies have also embraced the modding community. Erica Synths recently released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine, Polyend open-sourced its line of Tracker grooveboxes, and Behringer has also announced a slew of open-source devices, including a $150 clone of the MPC One called Kick, a clone of the E-mu SP-1200, the Anima DJ controller, the Ignite sequencer, and the Polykeys 61 MIDI controller.
The change in the industry has been quick and seismic. O’Donnell said of the need to provide developers tools for hacking inMusic’s products, “I can tell you it wasn’t on our task list five weeks ago. It just all of a sudden has to be on a task list now.”
Of course, not everyone is thrilled. Elektron has expressed mixed feelings about the emergence of vibe-coded mods. The company banned linking to hacks and modified firmware from its official forums, though not discussing them generally, citing concerns about the possibility of damaging instruments. A statement posted on its forums says: “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them (potentially rendering them unusable), prevent future updates, affect warranty coverage.”
While Elektron doesn’t want people posting links to hacked Digitone firmware on its forums, it’s not actively trying to thwart the modding community. The consensus is there’s no going back now that vibe coding has upended the music gear world, and trying to stand in the way would be a mistake. inMusic’s O’Donnell told the Verge, “you can try to wall them off, which is just a losing battle one … and so we want to embrace them.”

Rune: A native GPU-rendered Rust UI framework for macOS, Windows, Linux and web
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

A native GPU-rendered Rust UI framework for macOS, Windows, Linux and the web, with its own renderer, text, layout and springs.
Every app can run headless, so an agent can render to PNG, dump the element tree and drive it with scripted input.
fn view(s: &State, _: &mut Cx<State>) -> El {
    let t = tok::theme(true);
    let label = text(if s.on { "Lights on" } else { "Lights off" })
        .font(type_::TITLE).color(t.text);
    let knob = el().key("knob").size(18.0, 18.0).radius(9.0).fill(t.knob)
        .absolute(if s.on { 18.0 } else { 2.0 }, 2.0);
    let switch = el().key("switch").role("switch").label("Lights").checked(s.on)
        .focusable(true).size(38.0, 22.0).radius(11.0)
        .fill(if s.on { tok::accent(0, true) } else { t.control_off })
        .motion(motion::SNAPPY)
        .on_press(|s: &mut State| s.on = !s.on)
        .child(knob);
    col().w_full().h_full().center().gap(16.0).fill(t.bg).child(label).child(switch)
}

Scriptable GeoDNS: Leaving AWS for Bunny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:15:03 UTC
01:15:03 KST

Scriptable GeoDNS: leaving AWS for Bunny
Vincent Bernat
To optimize the performance metrics of this blog, I relied on Amazon CloudFront to serve the assets,1 and Route 53 for the geo-aware DNS2 to direct readers to the closest host serving the content. But Route 53 is expensive: US$0.50 per zone per month, US$0.70 per million geolocation queries, and US$0.75 per healthcheck per month[1], plus US$1 per month for the KMS key[2] needed to sign zones with DNSSEC. When I discovered that Bunny DNS is almost free[3] for up to 500 domains and features scriptable answers, I made the jump! Plus, it’s a European company based in Slovenia.
Bunny CDN#
Bunny.net[4] started as BunnyCDN in 2015[5]. They added IPv6
support in 2017[6]. Switching was uneventful. I don’t bring a custom domain: I
serve the content from the b-cdn.net domain. As I depend on content
negotiation to serve AVIF and WebP images[7], I configure the CDN to cache
each image format separately[8].
I disable logging[9] to avoid collecting personal information. While the bunny.net GDPR page[10] promises they anonymize data, it is unclear what CloudFront keeps in its own logs when logging is disabled.
The only downside of the bunny.net CDN offering is the lack of HTTP/3. I asked their support: two minutes later, they answered they are working on it but have no ETA to share.
Bunny DNS#
Bunny.net introduced their DNS offering in 2022[11] and recently reduced its cost to almost zero[3]. They support geographical routing[12], but a very cool feature is the scriptable DNS[13]: it runs a piece of user-supplied JavaScript on each query to compute the answer.
I run seven small NixOS virtual machines to host this blog around the world: Paris, Nuremberg, Ashburn, Singapore, San Jose, São Paulo, and Sydney. Bunny’s scriptable DNS lets me return the IP addresses of the two nearest servers. The browser falls back to the second server if the first one is down.
const servers = [
  {
    ipv4: "45.90.160.60",
    ipv6: "2a0c:8881:5:100::1",
    latitude: 48.88,
    longitude: 2.22,
  },
  /* […] */
  {
    ipv4: "139.180.162.114",
    ipv6: "2001:19f0:5800:1855:5400:6ff:fef0:4c0a",
    latitude: -33.87,
    longitude: 151.21,
  },
];
const families = { A: "ipv4", AAAA: "ipv6" };
const records = { A: ARecord, AAAA: AaaaRecord };
export default function handleQuery(query) {
  const type = String(query.request.queryType).toUpperCase();
  const family = families[type];
  if (!family) return [];
  // Get user location
  const location = query.request.geoLocation;
  // Build a list of candidates
  let candidates = servers.map(
    (s) => new Server(s[family], s.latitude, s.longitude, 100),
  );
  // Select the two closest alive servers
  const selected = [];
  while (selected.length < 2) {
    const server = RoutingEngine.getClosestServer(candidates, location, true);
    selected.push(server);
    candidates = candidates.filter((s) => s.ip !== server.ip);
  }
  // Return their IP addresses
  return selected.map((s) => new records[type](s.ip, 3600));
}
The above script relies on the
RoutingEngine.getClosestServer()[14] helper, which returns the
closest alive3 server to the user.4 Thanks to Doggo[15], we can
check it works as expected, at least for A:5
$ doggo --gp-from="Amsterdam" A vincent.bernat.ch
LOCATION          NAME                TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
Amsterdam, NL
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  45.90.160.60
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  116.203.18.48
$ doggo --gp-from="Texas" A vincent.bernat.ch
LOCATION          NAME                TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
Houston (TX), US
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  5.161.44.145
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  149.28.219.155
The most annoying drawback of this method is that a user from Buenos Aires gets both São Paulo (1000 mi, 30 ms RTT) and Ashburn (5200 mi, 140 ms RTT). Most resolvers randomize the order, so the user may pull the web page from Ashburn. We could return only the nearest server—and swap the scripted record with the built-in geographic routing instead. But if the server becomes unavailable, the browser has no alternative until the DNS cache expires. It leaves a short window of unavailability, even with a short TTL.
The HTTPS record solution#
The HTTPS DNS record[19], defined in RFC 9460[20], solves both the availability and the latency issues. Modern browsers query this record to get additional information to reach an HTTP server, including an alternative port and the application layer protocol—HTTP/2 or HTTP/3. Each record has a priority. We can ask browsers to contact the nearest server first and fall back to the next one if the first is unavailable:
vincent    HTTPS  1 first.geo  alpn="h3,h2"
vincent    HTTPS  2 second.geo alpn="h3,h2"
vincent    HTTPS  3 .          alpn="h3,h2"
; Bunny DNS must provide the two closest servers as "first.geo"
; and "second.geo" with geographic or latency routing.
first.geo  A      45.90.160.60
first.geo  AAAA   2a0c:8881:5:100::1
second.geo A      116.203.18.48
second.geo AAAA   2a01:4f8:1c0c:5eb5::1
vincent    A      45.90.160.60
vincent    A      116.203.18.48
vincent    AAAA   2a0c:8881:5:100::1
vincent    AAAA   2a01:4f8:1c0c:5eb5::1
This looks like the ideal solution! Unfortunately, Chrome ignores any record
whose target is not .[21], hence the last record at priority 3.
Moreover, unlike with a CNAME, Bunny DNS does not return the IP addresses for
first.geo and second.geo in the additional section. The resolver needs to
send a first request to get the HTTPS record, and a second to resolve
first.geo.
HTTPS records are still too new[22] for this use case. Back to the drawing board! 📐
The hybrid solution#
As a compromise, the script returns the two nearest servers if they are at a similar distance from the user. Otherwise, it returns only the nearest one with a lower TTL of 2 minutes.
export default function handleQuery(query) {
  const location = query.request.geoLocation;
  let candidates = servers.map(
    (s) => new Server(s.ipv4, s.latitude, s.longitude, 100),
  );
  // Select the two closest servers
  const selected = [];
  while (selected.length < 2) {
    const server = RoutingEngine.getClosestServer(candidates, location, true);
    selected.push(server);
    candidates = candidates.filter((s) => s.ip !== server.ip);
  }
  // Compute the distance to the user for each of them
  const [first, second] = selected.map((s) =>
    GeoDistance.calculate(s, location),
  );
  // If the second one is at twice the distance and at more than 1000 miles
  // from the first, return only the first one with a TTL of 2 minutes.
  if (second > 2 * first && second - first > 1000) {
    return [new ARecord(selected[0].ip, 120)];
  }
  // Otherwise, return both with a TTL of 1 hour.
  return selected.map((s) => new ARecord(s.ip, 3600));
}
We can check it with Doggo. From Chicago, we get only the Ashburn server with a TTL of 2 minutes, while from Mexico, we get both Ashburn and San Jose.
$ doggo --gp-from="Chicago" A vincent.bernat.ch
LOCATION          NAME                TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
Chicago (IL), US
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     120s   5.161.44.145
$ doggo --gp-from="Mexico" A vincent.bernat.ch
LOCATION          NAME                TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
Queretaro, MX
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  5.161.44.145
                  vincent.bernat.ch.  A     3600s  149.28.219.155
$ doggo --reverse 5.161.44.145 149.28.219.155
NAME                          TYPE  TTL    ADDRESS
145.44.161.5.in-addr.arpa.    PTR   7187s  web05.luffy.cx.
155.219.28.149.in-addr.arpa.  PTR   3600s  web07.luffy.cx.
Note
On the live page[23], the map below is interactive: point at a location to get the DNS answer, or disable servers to see how the answers change.
Note
Enable JavaScript to make the map below interactive: point at a location to get the DNS answer, or disable servers to see how the answers change.

location!
The complete code[18] is a bit more complex. It works around
RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() supporting only IPv4, and it handles the case
where there are not enough alive servers to build an answer.
Bunny.net has a comprehensive Terraform provider[24]. I leverage CDK Terrain[25] to build the target state in TypeScript and OpenTofu[26] to deploy it. Have a look at “Managing infrastructure with Terraform, CDKTF, and NixOS[27]” for more details.6
ACME DNS with Hickory DNS#
Route 53 covered one additional use case of mine: serving acme.luffy.cx to
solve DNS-01 ACME challenges[29]. Unlike Route 53, Bunny DNS cannot
restrict access to a single zone with a fine-grained access policy. As this
usage requires neither high availability nor low latency, I replaced Route 53
with Hickory[30], a memory-safe DNS server written in Rust. It supports
automatic DNSSEC signatures[31] and dynamic updates[32]. Its
configuration is simple:
[[zones]]
zone = "acme.luffy.cx"
zone_type = "Primary"
[zones.stores]
allow_update = true
type = "sqlite"
journal_path = "acme.luffy.cx.sqlite"
zone_path = "acme.luffy.cx.zone"
# Private key to sign the zone with DNSSEC. Generated with:
#  openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256
[[zones.keys]]
algorithm = "ECDSAP256SHA256"
key_path = "/etc/hickory-dns.acme.luffy.cx.pem"
# TSIG key to sign zone updates. Generated with:
#  openssl rand 32
[[zones.stores.tsig_keys]]
algorithm = "hmac-sha256"
key_file = "/etc/hickory-dns.acme.luffy.cx.update.acme.luffy.cx.tsig"
name = "update.acme.luffy.cx."
The provided zone file[33] only seeds the database on first start. I delegate
DNS-01 challenges to this zone with CNAME records:
_acme-challenge          CNAME bernat.ch.acme.luffy.cx.
_acme-challenge.vincent  CNAME vincent.bernat.ch.acme.luffy.cx.
Lego[34], the ACME client I use to get certificates from Let’s Encrypt[35], answers the DNS-01 challenge by pushing entries with the DNS UPDATE protocol[36].
Unfortunately, Bunny DNS cannot publish a DS record in a zone.7 I need one
to secure the acme.luffy.cx zone and certificate delivery. Therefore, I host
the luffy.cx zone on deSEC[37],8 a free DNS hosting service run by a
non-profit organization based in Berlin. I derive the DS record to publish in
luffy.cx from the DNSKEY record of acme.luffy.cx:
$ ZONE=acme.luffy.cx
$ dig @nsupdate.luffy.cx $ZONE DNSKEY +noall +answer \
>   | dnssec-dsfromkey -a SHA-256 -f - $ZONE
acme.luffy.cx. IN DS 55628 13 2 4946E7508F20E15F1B577A231104B029A1A82E04699A80CD46ADCE31227EE81F
Overall, I am quite happy with the switch to bunny.net. There are still a few
rough edges, like the inability to publish DS records, the lack of HTTP/3, and
the IPv4-only RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() helper. The bill went from US$5
per month to US$1. So far, performance is on par with AWS[39], but I
only finalized the current setup, including the server in Sydney, in late
October. I need a bit more time to gather more data, and I’ll post a short update. 📈
Update (2026-11)
This post was briefly discussed on Hacker News[40].

Scriptable GeoDNS: Leaving AWS for Bunny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:15:03 UTC
01:15:03 KST

Scriptable GeoDNS: leaving AWS for Bunny
Vincent Bernat
To optimize the performance metrics of this blog, I relied on Amazon CloudFront to serve the assets,1 and Route 53 for the geo-aware DNS2 to direct readers to the closest host serving the content. But Route 53 is expensive: US$0.50 per zone per month, US$0.70 per million geolocation queries, and US$0.75 per healthcheck per month[1], plus US$1 per month for the KMS key[2] needed to sign zones with DNSSEC. When I discovered that Bunny DNS is almost free[3] for up to 500 domains and features scriptable answers, I made the jump! Plus, it’s a European company based in Slovenia.
Bunny CDN#
Bunny.net[4] started as BunnyCDN in 2015[5]. They added IPv6
support in 2017[6]. Switching was uneventful. I don’t bring a custom domain: I
serve the content from the b-cdn.net domain. As I depend on content
negotiation to serve AVIF and WebP images[7], I configure the CDN to cache
each image format separately[8].
I disable logging[9] to avoid collecting personal information. While the bunny.net GDPR page[10] promises they anonymize data, it is unclear what CloudFront keeps in its own logs when logging is disabled.
The only downside of the bunny.net CDN offering is the lack of HTTP/3. I asked their support: two minutes later, they answered they are working on it but have no ETA to share.
Bunny DNS#
Bunny.net introduced their DNS offering in 2022[11] and recently reduced its cost to almost zero[3]. They support geographical routing[12], but a very cool feature is the scriptable DNS[13]: it runs a piece of user-supplied JavaScript on each query to compute the answer.
I run seven small NixOS virtual machines to host this blog around the world: Paris, Nuremberg, Ashburn, Singapore, San Jose, São Paulo, and Sydney. Bunny’s scriptable DNS lets me return the IP addresses of the two nearest servers. The browser falls back to the second server if the first one is down.
