Promethevs: Full DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash-1017, locally, on 12GB of VRAM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:14:47 UTC
01:14:47 KST

The original model, not a smaller copy · 64 GB of RAM and one 12 GB NVIDIA card · free and open source
PROMETHEVS runs DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, one of the strongest open models, from all 510 GB of its original weights, on an ordinary PC that cannot even load it: a Ryzen 9 3950X with 64 GB of DDR4, an RTX 3060 with 12 GB and two NVMe drives.
The PROMETHEVS engine gets there with compress-then-correct, a method devised by Ryan Flavell. Every word is first computed on a 2-bit copy of the model's experts. When the model itself is unsure (its top two choices are close), that word is recomputed with the original weights, rebuilt exactly from a stored correction plane. You get close to the speed of the compressed copy and close to the answers of the full model.
- Full-model quality, counted. On 960 audited words the output picks the full model's word 98.3% of the time (the 2-bit copy alone: 97.4%).
- Up to 7.4 tokens/s on a code prompt (warm cache, best case), against 2.14 for running the full model exactly on the same PC. Server runs: 5 to 8 on code, 4.5 to 5.4 on reasoning and agent prompts.
- Fast follow-ups. Only the first read of a long prompt is slow; the engine keeps what it has read, so the next message in a conversation starts in about 2 seconds.
- Works with your tools. An OpenAI-compatible endpoint on localhost, with streaming and tool calls, so apps and coding agents that speak the OpenAI API can use it.
- Private. The model runs on your PC; your chats stay there.
- Built from the original weights, on your machine. The installer downloads DeepSeek's weights and builds every store itself, checked against published hashes, so you do not have to trust our files.
- Free. Engine Apache-2.0; report, figures and logs CC BY 4.0.
New here? Check what you need, then install.
The hardware check in the bundle tests all of this and tells you up front if anything falls short. The full list is in engine-0.2/INSTALL.md.
- Download PROMETHEVS_0.2.zip from the latest release and extract it, for example to C:\promethevs_pkg.
- In PowerShell, from that folder:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\check_hardware.ps1        # checks the PC, picks the drives
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\build_stores.ps1 --run    # downloads the weights, builds the stores (resumable)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\start_engine.ps1          # starts the engine (about 1 minute)
python scripts\py\verify_install.py --speed                                # checks it and measures the speed
- Point any OpenAI-compatible app at http://127.0.0.1:8100/v1, model deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-promethevs, any non-empty API key. Close other programs that use the graphics card first.
Every step, the time and disk each one takes, and the known gaps are in engine-0.2/INSTALL.md. Release notes: engine-0.2/RELEASE_NOTES_0.2.md.
Measured on the build machine, 160 new tokens per prompt, two passes per run. Cold is a pass that starts with an empty expert cache. Warm is the second pass of the same prompt with the cache kept from the first, which is the best case for a cache; a real session that sends a different prompt lies between the two. Every individual run is in RESULTS.md.
Agreement is measured word by word against the word the exact path would choose given the same history. A slip is a difference the engine did not check, because the model was confident; the unchecked count counts those. Counting every difference also includes the words the engine checked and deliberately kept at a near-tie (both words almost equally likely). On its own the 2-bit copy picks the full-weight word on 97.4 percent of words; with the corrections, 98.33 percent counting every difference (99.17 percent by the unchecked count). The engine differs from the baseline build in two ways: it holds the draft head's experts in the 2-bit format too, and it keeps the expert cache from the first pass into the second. Keeping the cache lifted the code prompt but not the reasoning or agent prompts (the report gives the round timers behind this). In all three warm code passes no correction overturned a word, so the cache, the 2-bit draft head and the absence of an overturn are not separated, and 7.4 is a best case, not a typical session.
The PROMETHEVS engine does four things at once.
A 2-bit copy answers every word. The experts are stored in a 2-bit format that is smaller than the original FP4, so each word needs fewer bytes from disk. That is what makes the machine fast enough to be useful.
The model's own confidence picks the words to redo. For each word the engine looks at the gap between the model's top two candidates. When the gap falls below a threshold, the gate (0.45 here), the word is flagged.
Flagged words are corrected exactly. A stored correction plane turns an expert's 2-bit copy back into the exact FP4 expert, so a correction is the full model's answer for that word.
A draft head proposes several words at a time. DeepSeek ships a draft head with the model. The engine checks its guesses together in parallel lanes, which spreads the cost of reading experts across several words. The experts the model uses most sit in GPU memory; the rest live in RAM and on the two drives.
The method is compress-then-correct, devised by Ryan Flavell; the PROMETHEVS engine is built around it. Speculative decoding, quantised drafts and offloaded mixture-of-experts inference are the work it builds on; the report sets the method beside the closest references.
The build machine is a Windows 11 desktop with 64 GB DDR4, an RTX 3060 12 GB, and two NVMe drives (2 TB and 1 TB). The stores need about 1,009 GiB: 475 GiB of raw weights plus 534 GiB of derived stores (2-bit copies, correction planes, and FP4 copies of the first layers). Disk is the largest barrier for anyone repeating this. We kept each drive below about 90 percent full.
Every number above comes from one PC. If you run release 0.2 on your own machine, please send the output of python scripts\py\verify_install.py --speed and your engine log as a benchmark report. Reports are added here as they arrive.
Frontier-level AI today needs either a cloud subscription or hardware costing tens of thousands of pounds. Open-weight models are closing the gap with the closed frontier models, but running them still means someone else's server. PROMETHEVS, named after Prometheus, who in the myth brought fire to people, sets out to change that: frontier capability, at a speed close to the cloud, within 97 percent of what the original full weights would say, on a computer people already own. Release 0.1 published the method and every measurement; release 0.2 lets you run it.

The report (PDF, Markdown) sets out the method, the measurements, where the time goes, what did not help and the related work. Every run behind it is listed in RESULTS.md, with the unedited logs in logs/.

We measured agreement against our own exact path; we have not yet run DeepSeek's reference implementation side by side. Speeds vary by prompt and by run, so we give every run. No prompt reaches the 8 tokens/s milestone we set, and the reasoning and agent prompts run below 5.3. First-word time on long prompts is read-bound: on a 1,163-token prompt the first word arrives after about 126 s (98 s with a candidate prompt-reading setting whose effect on quality we have not fully measured). The 99.17 percent figure covers three prompts of 30, 76 and 1,163 tokens. On a further 1,101-token agent prompt the engine scores 97.80 percent and the baseline build 97.16 (9 slips in 317 words), 0.16 points above our 97 percent contract at the gate we use (at gate 0.30 it falls to 96.21 percent); on a 4,288-token prompt the engine scores 100 percent and the baseline build 99.69. Counting every difference, both builds fall below 97 percent on the 1,101-token prompt (95.91 and 95.58 percent). Each long-prompt audit is one run. The chat template matches DeepSeek's encoder on six plain conversations; tool results and thinking mode are unchecked. All numbers come from one machine, one model and one prompt family.
REPRO.md outlines the steps we ran: download and verify the weights, build the stores, set the profile, run the benchmark. The scripts themselves ship in release 0.2 (PROMETHEVS_0.2.zip, see engine-0.2/INSTALL.md).

Fox completes its $22B acquisition of Roku
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-06
16:05:36 UTC
01:05:36 KST

Fox has completed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, wrapping up one of the biggest media deals in recent years and giving the company a major boost in the streaming and connected TV space.
Announced Friday, the deal brings the streaming company founded in 2002 formally under Fox’s ownership. Fox says the combined company now ranks as the third-largest television business in the U.S. by viewership.
“We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today. What does change is our reach and resources,” Roku founder Anthony Wood said in a statement. “Our teams will keep building and innovating as they always have, now with the support and capabilities of Fox behind us.”
For Fox, the move provides direct access to Roku’s reach of more than 100 million households. The company expects that audience to help it improve advertising targeting, strengthen its position in the fast-growing connected TV market, and reduce its reliance on traditional TV distribution.
Today’s announcement comes two months after the Justice Department issued a second request for information, asking both companies to provide additional data and documents as part of its antitrust review. Earlier this month, reports suggested the deal was nearing U.S. regulatory approval.
The acquisition also closed much earlier than expected. When the deal was first announced in June, the companies projected it would be completed in the first half of 2027.

How the S-1 talks about existential risk
Zvi: Yeah. So as usual, when I look at anything from Anthropic, I want to see their attitude towards existential risk, alignment, whether or not they're going to potentially kill everyone.
So in this case, they mention existential risk only in passing, only in the passive voice. They're clearly trying to have it both ways. When they talk to the investors, they want to say, "Oh, look at our big mission, but our big mission is to build this super profitable hypercomputing thing." And then other times they want to say, "Our geniuses in the data center actually might kill everyone," and these two things have to coexist.
Similarly, pacing the frontier is something they do talk about here, but then they make clear to investors, "Don't worry. When we said pacing the frontier, we did not mean not making incredibly fast AI progress. We did not mean voluntarily let someone else go first. We just meant it would be great if everybody could collectively agree to go only at super speed and not at ludicrous speed." But they will do the embedded evaluations.
Similarly, we're all worried about recursive self-improvement. And here they call that "closing the loop" to be more business-friendly, but they say that their entire business model is they want to close the loop. They are worried that if someone else closes the loop before they close the loop, they will be out of the loop and they will lose.
So they intend to close the loop as fast as possible and as much as possible.
Patrick: I feel like there is an interesting tension around S-1s, because we largely have this culture in the tech industry of, necessarily, Zuck speaks for Facebook and Facebook speaks for Zuck. Tech has done complicated innovations with share classes that enable the founder/company relationship to be relatively durable over a period of years and decades.
[Patrick notes: Facebook was not the first company to issue super-voting founder shares but it popularized the model. Pattern matching goes both ways with Silicon Valley investors: you should believe your new investment is the second coming of Facebook. If you don’t, stop now; returns in venture are heavily weighted towards a handful of generational companies, and the entire game is spreading out your fund such that you are definitely in them and persuading the founder that you will be easy to work with (and so please don’t cut your allocation in any round). If you believe you are investing in the next Facebook, you affirmatively want the next Zuck at the helm durably regardless of how diluted their economic stake gets as they raise capital. Public market investors, seeing a company which grew from a dorm room to a global power, largely seem to accept precedent on provisions guaranteeing founder control. If founders have them at IPO, they keep them.]

But when you get the quote-unquote "responsible adults" in the room — S-1s are largely drafted by external counsel and counsel working for the banks that are the underwriters of the S-1.
Responsible adults say: "We all understand that everyone in the tech industry thinks that the CEO runs the company. However, managerial capitalism says that the CEO only runs the company to the extent that they're not fired by the board on behalf of the shareholders.
And while you've taken some amount of effort to make sure that that never happens, we have to pretend that in principle it is possible that it happens, and so we can't privilege the CEO's voice among many other voices." Patrick: And there's also liability-minimization happening here, where lawyers will always advise you, "Don't say anything that you don't need to say. [Patrick notes: I believe this factor is underrated. Consider a very prosaic lawsuit about an ordinary corporate matter. And my view essentially is that if we do too much of that, there's a very good chance that in fact AI will kill everyone, either from Anthropic or otherwise. And the argument that, "Oh no, this is the place where we have to say it in a way that matters, therefore we shouldn't say it the way that you want to say it" — well, I say that's exactly my reason why you should say it there, and why, if you choose not to make a costly signal, you've told me who you are. Founder control and Anthropic's share classes
Patrick: Cool. Shall we go to the second part of your takeaways, which was on control, I think?
Zvi: Anthropic has long had an attitude, like many tech companies, as you point out, that the founders should continue to control the company, and that the worst thing that could happen to Anthropic would be to have the likes of Google and Amazon suddenly having them maximize shareholder value and then thinking about only corporate things. And then their company would probably go out there and increase the risk that the world is destroyed, and lose their unique company culture, and this would be extremely bad.
So to that end, Anthropic has a very weird structure that they made even weirder in advance of the IPO. They have the one Class F share that belongs to the founders, and the founders collectively vote on how to exercise that share. And that share has 50.1% of the voting power for a wide range of issues, which is another way of saying the founders will keep control of the company as long as at least three of the founders continue to show up to the company, which could last quite a long time.
Anthropic's anticipation is this will last until long after the fate of the world has been decided one way or another. And this seems rather likely, because there are something like nine of them, and only three of them have to keep showing up.

And a default assumption would be that the Class E shares would side with the founders.
Patrick: I don't think I've ever heard of another company explicitly privileging employees with share classes. Generally, it's something of the reverse.
[Patrick notes: Employees most typically get stock options or restricted stock units which are designed to convert into common stock, or into a second class of common that is economically identical and differs only in voting, with the distinction typically disappearing after IPO or sale. Companies sometimes offer employees inducements to impair their stock in some way, such as accepting a voting proxy agreement (ceding their votes to the founders) in return for e.g. better-than-market exercise terms for their options.
Common shares vote like Republicans in Chicago: mathematically you have no say in outcomes, but you do have a right to have your opinion tallied.]

The traditional thing to do in the tech industry is to have the employees proxy their votes to the founders, and the founders literally get to vote them in whichever way they want. And you're, in doing this, suggesting, "No, I think the employees are sufficiently philosophically aligned with management that they will proxy without a proxy agreement being in place," which is an interesting point of view.
And I'm not saying "interesting" as a way of saying I don't think it is well-calibrated. [Patrick notes: Many companies experience, after hypergrowth, discontent among long-time employees (and sometimes founders) that the company has lost something special in the culture. You then intentionally, as a mechanical consequence of hypergrowth and with your eyes open, hired 10 people with impeccable credentials from AppAmaGooBookSoft for every one who previously worked with you. You will always find your culture drawn to the median culture of AppAmaGooBookSoft as a result of this choice. You will be warned about it in advance, and you will say “It will not happen here!” It will happen to you. It happened to AppAmaGooBookSoft, too.]
Patrick continues: Not that there is another company at that revenue growth rate to point to, but we will get to that in a moment, I think.
Zvi: Well, so before we move on, I would say Anthropic has long cultivated a very special company culture that has a large awareness of safety, but also of altruistic goals and charity and making the world a better place.
The founders have famously pledged 80% of their shares to charity, and they've offered very, very generous matching donations for those who want to give their stock away. And in fact, how much stock you gave away determines how many Class E shares you have to vote. So they're, on several levels, determining, no, these are the preselected people who have very, very costly signaled that they want to influence the future in generally good ways, rather than build personal wealth and maximize profits.
Those are the people who will ultimately make the tie-breaking vote in this situation, and that is exactly what that was selected for.
Anthropic's uncapped donation matching
Patrick: I couldn't find if this was explicitly called out in the S-1, and I will edit the transcript if I missed it in my first two readings. But their matching program for employees might be one of the most expensive single corporate decisions ever made in the history of capitalism.
The matching program for employees was, I hear, calibrated to essentially allow employees to do something similar to what the founders were doing, and give away 80% of their economic stake. And to make those numbers work, they said that the corporation will basically match employee donations on a 3:1 basis, which is unheard of in the rest of capitalism.
And additionally, typically a corporate matching program is: okay, we will match on a one-to-one basis up to, let's say, $7,000 a year. And so you say, okay, well, optimally executed, that option is worth $7,000 to charity, and perhaps $10,000, $11,000 or so in pre-tax income. The Anthropic matching program is uncapped.
And so there are employees that will donate $20 million to charity and have it get backed by $60 million of Anthropic money in the wake of the IPO and their continued operation and similar. And when you sum that over extremely charitably minded employees, times thousands of them, times many of them that have presumptively eight- and nine-figure equity values, which they will quickly be giving away, that is just going to be an extremely expensive decision.
Zvi: Yeah, but they got what they wanted out of it. You want to strongly differentiate yourself as an employer and attract aligned employees.
If you're not committed to the mission, it sounds expensive, but if you are mission-aligned, the expense is a positive. And when you turn out to be the fastest-growing company in history, and the stock is worth close to $2 trillion, it will be a larger line item than you thought.
But at the same time, you'll be able to afford it conditional on success, so it works both ways.
Postscript: what the matching program will actually cost
Patrick injects via new recording: I failed at Ctrl+F prior to recording. The S-1 does indeed mention the donation matching program in a few places. For example, it says that the Class N shares are reserved against the need to make good on these commitments, and the company took a $2 billion non-cash charge in Q3 related to it.
So in terms of cash, the matching program will be close to free. Shareholders as a class, inclusive of donors, pay for it through dilution. In terms of accounting, though, when you promise people compensation worth billions of dollars, we want to record the fact that you have promised billions of dollars.
When you promise them compensation based on future world states, we update the cost of that promise as we learn more about the future. I suspect the Q3 charge is very far from the last non-cash charge attributable to the matching program. Future charges will happen as employees make new pledges, as past pledges not yet settled get remarked from a 409A valuation to the public price, and, probably the dominant factor, as currently pledged equity continues to vest and gets matched at public market prices rather than the private ones.
The S-1 suggests there is presently about $24 billion in unvested equity compensation, with that calculation being made as of the day the equity was granted. When the cost of the match is calculated, it is calculated the day the equity vests, which will probably be at a higher valuation.
And then you assume that much of the equity is going to employees eligible for three-to-one matching at the new mark, and much of the remainder to employees eligible for one-to-one matching at the new mark, and that probably tens of percent of it will be donated. And so, yep, that is almost certainly the most expensive perk in the history of capitalism.
I suspect the magnitude of the first post-IPO charges is going to surprise people. Much has been written, including by my former colleague Nan, of the coming tidal wave of charitable donations. A large portion of that tidal wave flows through Anthropic's P&L.
Revenue growth and cohort economics
Zvi: So the next section of questions is about money, of course.
So Anthropic is one of the fastest-growing companies in history. We're talking about 10x year over year for several years in a row. We're talking, in some places, even greater than that. First two quarters this year were completely nuts.
Patrick: About 15x in the first half, right?
[Patrick notes: $1.16 billion in H1 2025 to $16.3 billion in H1 2026, so about 14x, though what is one entire prior-year half between friends.]
Zvi: Right. Approximately, something like that, 15x in the first half, from a very large baseline to begin with, rather than from very small amounts.
I mean, in the beginning it was like, okay, you're 10x-ing, but this is not unheard of because it's a very small company. Now it's a relatively large company, and people are asking questions like, how many times can you 10x? The entire economy is only so big. There are only so many Fortune 500 companies.
It's just 500. At some point you're going to run out of targets. But that's not necessarily something we're getting close to. Quarter three, they did slow their growth. So their growth was still the envy of almost every company on Earth, but by their own standards, it was reasonably small.
We have a variety of explanations for this. Anthropic was relatively badly positioned in terms of the quality of their available models and their appeal to business, compared to how they had been in the previous period or in the later period that we're in now. So that's probably my guess as to the main reason.
There's also some talk about quarter three just being a slow period for growth, relatively speaking, due to the calendar. But my expectation is that quarter three was relatively slow, but that quarter four has picked up again, and you will see some very, very large growth numbers out of Anthropic.
Patrick: In analysis of securities, we have to pretend that the gross quarter-to-quarter revenue results matter. But in this case, I think Anthropic is properly modeled more or less as a software company, where what you are doing is stacking cohorts together. And for reasons, we do not require software companies to break out their cohort numbers in S-1s and similar.
[Patrick notes: This is extremely well-understood among the best managers in the world, and relatively well-understood among investors. One classic articulation of it is Bezos’ in 2017, referencing a much slower-moving business which was once the fastest growing business of all time: “Those quarterly results were fully baked three years ago. So today I'm working on a quarter that will happen in 2020, not next quarter. Next quarter is done already and it's probably been done for a couple years.”]
If we did, that would be a fascinating window into the growth of the business. And so the cohorts are often heterogeneous with each other, and so the customers that you recruited in Q3 2026 are at a different point in their ramp of spend than the customers you recruited in Q3 2025, than in 2024.
And the very interesting thing that you would want to see on those graphs is: do they asymptote at any point? And finger to the wind, my guess is the answer is no. The S-1 says they have a net revenue retention of 900%, which is silly for any other SaaS business. If you were doing 110%, that would be wonderful.
[Patrick notes: Slight exaggeration; that’s workmanlike execution for an IPOable SaaS company selling on annual contracts.]
But my guess is their "early adopter customers," the ones that were there in the ancient history of two years ago, have not figured the limits of cognition in their businesses yet, and are continuing to pour money at tokens and get business results out. And if you were hypothetically in a world where a cohort graph would show that, okay, after the first two years of adoption, the growth pace goes to that of a normal software business, then you would be much more bearish on Anthropic and labs generally as a business.
I suspect we are not in that world. I suspect the line for people that have been on two years continues to be vertical, and it will look less vertical in the first three months of a customer's life, as they do things like internal pilots, IT starts to get involved, yada, yada, yada, all that fun stuff for the absorption of this technology in the world.
And so I suspect quarter-to-quarter softness in the number is more an artifact of how the cohort graphs stack up than it is an artifact of the total corporate positioning relative to competitors in that quarter. But I do not have internal numbers on this. Obviously, if I had internal numbers, I would not be able to share them.
Postscript: Q3 was a supply story, not a demand story
Patrick: After recording the episode, I thought through this a bit more, including with Claude assisting, and have a better hypothesis.
As I mentioned, it is useful to have lenses available, like being a SaaS-y guy, because it lets you see the world in terms of cohorts. It sometimes impairs your vision, though, because you imagine every business as having arbitrarily high margins and the ability to scale to customer demand as quickly as DevOps can type into their terminal.
Anthropic is, importantly, less like a software business in those respects. Anthropic says in the S-1, "We have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded the supply available to us." Their ability to service revenue from fully bought-in customers is limited by the contracted, racked, powered GPUs available to them.
The S-1 says historically they make these arrangements 12 to 18 months in advance. And so, in roughly Q1 or Q2 of 2025, they had to make a guess as to how compute efficient a yet-to-be-released Opus 5.5 would be, and how much customers would be willing to use it.
Anthropic seems to have underestimated or —in Zvi's parlance elsewhere—perhaps simply not to have been aggressive enough.
Their Q3 revenue softening isn't a demand story. It's a supply story. They're running all the GPUs they have, and it just isn't enough. Supporting evidence: they talk about hitting the spot market for GPUs for $5 billion, at substantially more than their multi-year commitments typically run, in such a way as to eat 10% of the margin just from the shift in the mix.
You'd assume low tens of percent of revenue is served by spot compute, but that spot compute made up 50% of their compute spend for the quarter. The S-1 says "short-term commitments," which might not line up one-to-one with, for example, how AWS will sell you a spot instance. Roll with me here on the lingo.
The important bit is that you're paying through the nose for availability as a trade-off for not contracting for that capacity in advance. And so why has the revenue softened? Either because you want to make the principled decision that you don't want to climb the cost curve in the spot market and sell at wafer-thin margins or for a loss just to inflate your top-line metrics, or perhaps because you just tapped all the spot that capitalism had available in Q3 2026.
I think analysts who read this as softening demand would need to explain tapping spot for 50% of one's spend. I frankly don't think there is an explanation available there. These analysts are just straightforwardly wrong. Even if one allocates all of the spot compute to training runs for Opus 6.x or whatever, that's still saying they fully saturated the long-term contracted chips, and their customers still had tokens waiting.
Is it a bubble?
Zvi: Yep, it's really hard to say. There's a lot of different factors. We have very low visibility, for a variety of obvious reasons. We have to endlessly hear the same people predict the imminent fall of OpenAI and Anthropic, and the imminent commodification of the models, and the imminent — everybody's going to stop spending so much on tokens.
And they say this every time the number 10xes, which has been a remarkably large number of times. And yes, at some point, number has gone up, and estimates of the future rate of number going up will go down, and therefore stock price will go down even as the token usage and the revenue numbers go up. And at that point, people will talk about the bubble bursting, and they will be wrong.
That is the default. Obviously, nothing I say is investment advice. As per usual, nothing you say is investment advice. But it's very easy to predict who will continuously predict these things happening and who will not.
Patrick: I think reasonably well-calibrated people could think, just on priors: I'm not paying much attention to what AI is doing. I've just heard this story before. Sizing the market for tokens
Patrick: Five years ago, I thought there is a reasonable chance that LLMs asymptote “just a bit higher than where we are today” on the capabilities curve. We'd have to hit an incredibly narrow bullseye for that to happen.
So I'm trying to update on evidence. There are some other people that have not really updated on that evidence. But even if we never got better than Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 — if this was the best it ever got, just waiting for this to roll out for the next couple of years in capitalism would make these some of the largest businesses by revenue in the economy.
Now, obviously they're structurally predicated on that not happening. But John Collison of Stripe — which previously employed me, and I'm not speaking on their behalf — had Sam Altman on John’s podcast Cheeky Pint a few days ago, and John said—and all of the following is my gloss rather than a quote—, plus or minus, round numbers, 1% of the entire operating expense of Stripe is AI tokens right now.
Asked what would the correct number be, I would describe John as hemming and hawing a bit, and then he suggested it would be in the tens of percent of OpEx.

The commodification bear case
Zvi: The bear case is essentially the expectation by many of commodification. It's the idea that, well, the cheaper, faster, open-weight, competitive models are going to be good enough for whatever you want to do.
You will choose to use them instead. If Anthropic's models don't get better, then a year from now, they would think, well, okay, at that point, the DeepSeek model or the Qwen model will be almost as good, and it will be cheaper and faster. So if all that Anthropic does is make their own model cheaper and faster, this will destroy their revenue margins, and their business will no longer function.
But there's no longer a case of, oh, AI doesn't do much, and the economy will adopt almost no AI. Again, even if AI is the minimum it could possibly be, and we never see another release that's any good again, and Carbon turns out to be terrible, and Fable 5.5 turns out to be a disappointment, and we go from there, and so on and so forth.
Cash efficiency and $800 billion in compute commitments
Zvi: The other thing to know about Anthropic's financials is that Anthropic's financials are actually incredibly good for a startup that is growing at this kind of rate, especially one that just eats capital in various ways. Not on net. And they are directly profitable in the first half: cash flow of $3.9 billion positive.
Now, if you adjust for the convertible notes not having been converted yet, and therefore they have to be considered as losses every time the stock price goes up, they post an $80 billion loss from that. They've sold that stock. Amazon has not converted to stock, but for all practical purposes, Amazon just has stock in Anthropic. So we should be thinking of this in terms of, okay, that's just part of the company's cap table, and they shouldn't be charged for losses any more than we should charge for Dario's stock going up in value, and therefore having been a more valuable thing to give to Dario.
That is a very silly way to do accounting. And then the actual expenses that we have to look forward to are — Anthropic has compute commitments of roughly $800 billion.
Patrick: The one thing I would say with regards to them being incredibly cash efficient — and they have been incredibly cash efficient — is that there are ways to trade off cash and future promises in ways that matter, and they've done some excellent corporate finance.
And I'm not saying that as a criticism at all. This is just someone who enjoys the game looking at a team of people that are very, very good at the game. They have locked up compute for the next couple of years in a trade where both parties get something they want. Anthropic says, "We want a price, and we want availability," and the other party says, "Okay, we want a guaranteed spend over a number of years."
And so a way in which they keep their cash expenses in the current period low is to say, "Okay, we're going to smear out a very large commitment over the next couple of years," and they're up to, I think the number is about $800 billion in commitments going forward. I think a midwit way to look at that is, well, that's equivalent to having $800 billion of debt, just like it would be if you had $800 billion of real estate leases. [Patrick notes: The conventional way to round $895 billion is to $900 billion but what is $95 billion between friends.]
I have reasons for not thinking that, but what's your perspective on the forward commits?
Zvi: So Anthropic has been incredibly conservative, in my opinion, on its forward commitments and its acquisition of compute. OpenAI has been much, much more aggressive. And still, OpenAI proved to be more conservative than it would have been optimal to have been, as things played out.
But you are trying to guard the downside option. And Anthropic has basically been saying, "Oh, we don't want to go broke and suddenly be in this position if growth is only very good and not insane." That didn't happen. But if it had, it is not clear to me that not having bought enough compute would have saved things that were that valuable. Whereas the cost of not having the compute available when things go really well is very high. Obviously, there are reasons to want to be risk-averse, but I do think they played it too conservatively, even though from an outside perspective, oh, $800 billion of forward commits, that's completely insane.
That's over a number of years. Compute is growing rapidly. AI is growing rapidly. The only way this works out badly for them is if the price of compute actively goes down substantially, so they can't resell it, and there's no demand for it. Postscript: what happens if the commits go bad
Patrick: Hideho, folks. So, a bit of a post-interview riff on this topic. There's an old saw: if you owe the bank $900, you have a problem. If you owe the bank almost $900 billion, the bank has a problem.
What does a future look like in which the buyer is unhappy about the $900 billion in forward commits? The most likely future is one with globally soft compute prices. You get there via some combination of: A, a supply glut of powered and racked GPUs because of capital overshooting demand.
B, major improvements in inference-time compute efficiency. C, a saturation of current approaches to intelligence, such that new training runs don't improve economic impact and are therefore shelved. D, policy restrictions on the amount of compute that can be put into training, or perhaps, less likely, inference.
Or E, a large decrease in global demand for cognition. I think you need to imagine some improbable world states to get there, but perhaps one gets there. Okay. What does one do with the commits then? Does one proceed straight to bankruptcy, like, for example, WeWork eventually did to get out from under many billions of dollars of now-uneconomic leases? No.
[Patrick notes: I had WeWork bonds, believing that they could refinance their way through unattractive leases using excellent access to the Japanese capital markets. Many investors would say, for career risk reasons, that the trade was blown up by the pandemic, but I think it was probably mistaken the day I made it. Anyhow, when you owe Softbank twenty billion dollars, that is SoftBank’s problem.
SoftBank is, of course, financing a large slug of the AI infrastructure buildout. They once owned about 5% of a company which made gamer-focused GPUs. SoftBank exited that niche hardware business, keeping the large stake in the CPU designer, because obviously CPUs are more economically important than GPUs. SoftBank tried to sell the CPU company to the GPU people, but the deal died in anti-trust, because the U.S. authorities were worried about that the GPU company might become too important if it controlled CPUs. (CPUs are, of course, the chip that gets racked by the hundreds of thousands in data centers worldwide.) Chastened by the feds, the GPU company returned to focusing on their niche business, which is now worth approximately $4 trillion. Whether this accomplished the goals of advocates of a robust anti-trust policy, I will let them articulate.
Some might read SoftBank’s checkered investment history as a reason to be skeptical of anything they try to put tens of billions of dollars into. Personally, I think the broadest outline of their strategy is simply correct. Collecting the Internet tax in a developed country a) throws off a huge amount of cash b) requires ongoing access to capital markets for nationwide infrastructure refreshes every decade or so and c) is done as a business. You can either choose to operate a utility, or do something interesting with your life. Funding industrial revolutions is a high-variance game but you only have to be right once.]
First, you start using some of the contractual features of those commits. For the $120 billion, or $3 billion a month, commit to SpaceX, you point to the line in the contract that says cancelable on 90 days' notice. This buys you some breathing room, if for some reason your crystal ball says compute is now hyperabundant at better prices relative to your anticipated needs, and this is likely to continue.
Not enough breathing room? You break out the other contracts. Nscale, Lambda: we contracted to pay you once the compute was delivered. It turns out the future we've arrived at sucks for us. Bad news: it sucks for you a whole lot worse. We will of course pay when you deliver compute as agreed upon, but you need tens of billions of dollars of capital to successfully deliver that compute.
And we anticipate that if you look around right now, you may possibly be able to afford a ham sandwich. So our commitment to you is going to evaporate when you fail to deliver. Not enough yet? Okay. Then you start triggering the prearranged contractual provisions which allow you to pay rent with convertible notes rather than dollars.
That will get you a few tens of billions. Small beer here, but tens of billions of dollars can be real money. Is that still not enough? Then: Google, Amazon, Microsoft, our beloved suppliers that are also major shareholders, it turns out we want to play Let's Make a Deal. Here's the first sketch of the new deal.
You take an accounting hit against contracted revenue for a few quarters. In return, you are a larger chunk of our cap table than you expected to be. This structure is definitely not robust against all possible world states. Again, they contemplate material risk of the world ending. But it is clearly anticipated that perhaps we come to regret these deals in the future.
Flexing compute between training, inference and subleasing
Patrick: And this is true within the labs as well. They have a couple of dials on — I think the three classic buckets a lab breaks down its own compute into are training for their own models, inference for the customers' use of the models, and then what is number three? Post-training or alignment or whatever. I think it gets described as different things in different places.
Zvi: Yeah. I think of lab compute spend as roughly divided in half between a combination of internal use, pre-training and post-training on the one hand, and serving the models on the other.
Patrick: Yeah. And so hypothetically in the future, if demand for inference goes up, keeping compute constant, you can adjust for that by saying, "Okay, we'll accept some slowdown with regards to our next model release," or shoot for less in terms of top-end capabilities, or yada yada.
And if there is a slowdown in customer demand for the model, then you think, "Well, pack more features into the next one and spend more on training it." Or, you know, the third option is essentially: sublease your compute to other people that are making more valuable use of it.
This is not a new phenomenon in human experience. One of the reasons Amazon and Google, et cetera got so good at racking servers in the early days of quote-unquote cloud was they were basically the best in the economy at turning servers into revenue. But they got so good at racking them that then they discovered, wait, it is in fact not the case that you have to be the best in the economy at monetizing a server to afford an almost infinite number of servers.
[Patrick notes: Amazon and Google specialized in racking servers because they had problems nobody else did. Google had a high-margin worldwide software business. Amazon had a predictable demand spike on Black Friday/Cyber Monday so large it required inventing an engineering discipline.
They then found, essentially as an industrial byproduct, that they were the world’s best marginal operator of servers. They informed the rest of capitalism of this fact, enterprises shifted their workloads off-premises over the course of about a decade and a half, and the three hyperscalers (Amazon, Google, and Microsoft) printed money hats.
As one of their hundreds of cloud infrastructure product lines, they got into GPU hosting. The motivating use cases at the time of this decision included video codec conversion at global scale. This turned out to not be the most interesting pipeline you could run on a GPU.]
If we just clone-stamp these boxes out into the universe, Fortune 500 companies will shift their workloads over to here at the prices we can offer, and it would be a ludicrously high margin business for us. And so AWS is probably the most important business inside of Amazon. Google's compute business is reasonably important, et cetera, et cetera.
And so there is a possibility that all that is old is new again, where, even if hypothetically the direct use of the API is soft for a few quarters, then they can say, "Well, we're sitting on a mountain of compute right now, and other people will need to use that for their own purposes. We will sublet 10 or 20% of our compute hoard for the quarter at some price that is mutually amenable," and then see what the global diffusion of this technology is next quarter.
Zvi: Yeah, it's certainly an option, and I don't expect them to ever have to take it. But we spent a significant period of time where everyone was talking about the depreciation schedules on all the GPUs, and how, oh my God, this will only last for so many years, the value will go down, the business model doesn't work, they're counting on such thin margins, how could this possibly work?
And now, of course, we have the situation where there's so much demand for compute that these things are staying in business indefinitely. The prices, if anything, are going up over time rather than down, because as much as we are producing more compute every year than we did the year before, and therefore have much more compute in the ecosystem, it doesn't matter. The demand is growing much faster than supply.
Patrick: Yeah. My understanding of the last couple of years of history — which is imperfect, because being a semiconductor analyst is not actually my job — but we were acutely compute constrained for a while. And so one of the reasons to make these forward-looking commits was that if you didn't make the commit, you didn't get an allocation.
[Patrick notes: Anthropic says in the S-1 that it has been routinely constrained, for the entirety of their corporate existence, by lack of sufficient compute.]
And since everyone was constrained on the number of powered H100s that were available in the world, which is a large number, but not an infinite number, to stay in the game, you kind of had to commit to the future. But we will probably run all these chips until they burn out in place, and then replace them with new chips, and just continue doing that, because we are not close to discovering the maximum amount of economic value of substitute intelligence, or substitute cognition, maybe.

Circular financing and the dot-com comparison
Patrick: So we've talked about their sort of capital stack issues.

Obviously, they're raising additional money through issuance of common stock in the IPO. There's also capital raising happening essentially across the tech industry to support this build-out, because we are in the midst of what is frankly an industrial revolution.
To the extent that Wall Street is worried about things going badly, I think they're worried about a symptom that we have seen before, where, through complicated shenanigans — either with a central actor, or through just individual participants in the market making locally rational decisions and ending up in a globally irrational place —
If you find a way to turn capital into revenue, and you loop that very quickly, sometimes things get to crazy places. And so a classic example of this is the interplay between Yahoo and the other startups shortly prior to the dot-com bust, where Yahoo's share price was increasing rapidly.
People treated that as the index price for the future value of the Internet. And startups would raise, saying, "Look at Yahoo's share price rising. You should bet on us as being part of this Internet land grab, and so assign a high valuation to us. We're going to take in that money. We will spend it on, of course, Yahoo ads, because that is the way to get users."
Spending money on Yahoo ads increases Yahoo’s revenue… which increases Yahoo’s share price… which increases investor interest in funding Internet startups… who promptly spend the money on Yahoo ads.
And then this cycle happens a few times, and we get a bit ahead of our skis. And so there is a complicated industrial apparatus happening right now in, again, a build-out for the ages. We are living through history in this moment. And one bit of that complexity is that the shareholders, Amazon and Google, are also major suppliers, are also major customers in some fashions, et cetera, et cetera.
And I think there is a sense in some people on Wall Street that there is a circularity here that could end badly. I don't think I share that point of view, but to the extent that there are credible bear cases, I think that is probably the intellectual scaffolding for the credible bear case.
Zvi: Yeah, I think it's a reasonable thing to be worried about from the outside view.
I think that, based on my understanding of the technology and what's happening, I am much less worried about it than I would be if I hadn't invested a lot of intellectual effort in this question, but it's certainly possible. It's certainly possible that something like a debt crisis could affect the industry.
The world is being asked to provide quite a lot of debt in ways that are really unprecedented. I certainly understand why you would do that. These companies are increasing in value rapidly. You don't really want to sell more stock than you have to. So it's certainly reasonable.
And another way of thinking about it is, if you are trying to efficiently raise capital and efficiently allocate capital and efficiently do an industrial revolution, the proper amount of risk of a crisis situation due to being a little bit over your skis on the revenue assumptions and the circularity is very much not zero.

Industrial revolutions and how weird the future gets
Patrick: I will say there is a bit of an intermediate, where, even if one doesn't credit fundamental transformation of the economy, the way industrial revolutions work is you redevelop entire supply chains to take advantage of the new thing. And so the kind of fundamental impact of the automobile versus horse-drawn carriages is not: people will be able to take a lot of long road trips across the United States — although that is one impact of it.
But it's like, no, substantially all transportation of goods and services will no longer go by horse. And we will take advantage of this, over a period of decades, to redraw the interlinkages of the economy. And there will be impacts of that in agriculture, in finance, in et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.
And these will be iterated and looped and interconnected in ways that are very difficult to understand when you see the first Model T roll off the assembly line and say, "Yeah, that is a really cool thing. I could see how that is going to play out." And we have very limited ability to see how it is going to play out right now.
[Patrick notes: The Model T doesn’t by itself imply the interstate highway system. Trucks carry the majority of America’s goods transportation, substantially enabled by that system. Long-haul trucking is one of the most common professions in the country; long-haul horsing is close to physiologically impossible. Long-haul trucking makes nationwide fast food chains viable, because it delivers bulk food system inputs year-round. And so, in a real way, the Model T changed what children grew up eating.]
The thing I keep going back to is, the future is going to be really, really weird. I think almost everybody is underestimating how weird the future is going to get. And certified Internet weirdos like you and I and some buddies of ours — I think we are probably underestimating how weird the future is going to get. Okay, I will say I am probably underestimating how weird the future is going to get.
Maybe taking the third pill helps you get to that. Maybe not.
Zvi: Yeah, I have successfully overshot on how weird it will get, how fast, in some ways. But the future is going to be really, really weird. And the present is in fact really, really weird. It's just that I managed to overshoot modestly on some of those questions.
And it is really disappointing, because it's just a microcosm of trying to warn about future dangers: even when we're talking about just future industrial processes, or future economic activity, future ordinary things, people measure AI almost always as, how do I slot the existing AI that exists today into the existing action that a human or a machine is currently doing, and have it substitute directly for the exact thing that's currently happening?
How good is it at that thing? And that is obviously a very small portion of what is going to happen. And that alone would in fact make the world really weird, but that is a very small fraction of the amount of weirdness that will happen, again, even if AI is relatively normal from here.
AI mathematics and the bitter lesson
Patrick: And it's frustrating, because we've already seen this happen enough that we can point to the recent past and say: if you thought the way AI was going to transform engineering was it was going to be the world's best autocomplete in existing IDEs — there are people that thought that, big bets placed on AI is going to make IDEs 20% more efficient than previously, and that will be a 10% increase in the aggregate output per engineer.
Twelve months after having that belief, you have, I would say, probably tens of percent of the engineering industry no longer booting up an IDE to do software development, because why would you? That would imply that you were looking at computer code. And the leading edge of the cool kids are just so far beyond that. Why would a cool kid have one’s main agent look at computer code when the swarm can look at computer code for him and save his context window?
We, over very short periods of time, get fundamental rethinkings of what the task looks like, done in very, very hard domains, and then it starts cranking through.
The field of mathematics is weird because the individual dollar value associated with mathematical breakthroughs is very low, but they're known to be pretty hard. And so, essentially as a marketing stunt, both labs have been just knocking down mathematical theorems, or producing proofs of hypotheses, et cetera, et cetera, with the same aplomb that SaaS businesses use to write blog posts.
And the math community feels very emotionally conflicted about this. And I think all of us are going to be emotionally conflicted about something coming in the next couple of years, to put it mildly. But the thing that generated that outcome was not that the chatbots are better at talking to a mathematician and driving hypotheses forward than any previous Wolfram Alpha has ever been.
It's like, no, this is the RSI, the recursive self-improvement. The agent swarm, with some amount of direction at problems, will just chat about it within themselves and essentially autonomously write out proofs that all the king's horses and all the king's men have not been able to come up with in the last several millennia, and then crank them out at such a rate that literally the entire field of research mathematics cannot check them as fast as they are being produced.
But there's good news. We're pretty confident that they're correct, because they come with formalizations, which is a thing that research mathematics doesn't normally ship with proofs, because it is some hundred-plus times more expensive than the proof itself. My mind is kind of blown. And this future is weird.
We're going to get our minds blown in so many things over the course of the next couple of years.
Zvi: Yeah, it's the bitter lesson. If you just make the things more capable, they will suddenly be able to do things, pretty much kind of automagically, kind of on their own, that you didn't expect them to be able to do.
You're suddenly like, "Oh, actually, the LLMs can drive." It's like, "The LLMs can drive?" Yeah, the LLMs can drive. What did you expect?

The hackening and who bears responsibility

I don't know whether it is reasonable to lay at their door consequences of decisions made by other people using their technology. I similarly don’t know whether it is reasonable to argue they simply didn't get distillation locked down quickly enough, and now they are in some way morally responsible for the consequences of that.
Zvi: I mean, I think that's a good point to close on: it's just sort of, it's not the incentives, it's you. And this goes to existential risk, and potentially building things that will lead to an AI race that gets everybody killed when we don't know how to control things that are smarter and more capable than ourselves, or when this creates equilibria that have no good solutions that we know of, and where all the natural outcomes are extremely bad.
And it also applies to hacks, where any individual decision makes sense, but inevitably goes down this road, and you didn't actually figure out how to mitigate this sufficiently. You didn't actually figure out how to fix it. And they've done some very commendable things, like Glasswing and Daybreak and so on, to try and mitigate the situation.
I'm sure it'd be vastly worse if they hadn't done those things. But at the end of the day, yeah, it's not the incentives, it's you. Don't pretend that just because someone else would've done it, that gives you the okay to do it, because then someone else is pointing at you.
Trapdoors and irreversible decisions
Patrick: I will say that there is an element of trapdoor-ness to — we are making decisions that are not fully reversible.
And that has been obvious for a few years, but there were, I think, many people involved who had reasonable points of view in a world where you think you would be able to have take-backs. And so there's many people in the tech industry, including many people who have dumped a lot of money into lobbying on this issue, who are quite committed to open source models being available as a thing.
And once the open source models and the open weights achieve a capability, that is the worst capabilities will ever be going forward, unless you successfully do a worldwide surveillance regime over all basic computing, which is hopefully impossible. It would be an incredibly dystopian world if we were able to blacklist mathematics.
So once it's out there, it's out there, and it is now out there with the capability of uplifting North Korea and other bad actors. And we will never be able to yank that back. We can only go forward from where we are right now. And I hope we learn the lesson of that with respect to things like — by the standards of things that AI could potentially do, stealing $5 billion from Binance is a prosaic risk.
There will be other trapdoors in the future, and we do not want to fall down those trapdoors as well. And I guess that is as good a place as any to call it. Well, Zvi, thanks very much for discussing. These days, your newsletter continues to be kind of essential for people trying to keep up on the frontier here.
Where can people find that?
Zvi: You can find my newsletter at thezvi.substack.com.
Patrick: Thanks very much for being on the program. And to everybody else out there, thanks very much for listening, and we'll see you next week on Complex Systems.

Sony Revives the Original Walkman Headphones, Adds USB-C (arstechnica.com) 25
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Sony has brought back the MDR-3-series headphones that debuted in 1979 alongside the Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player. [...] The new MDR-3R (originally called the "MDR-3L2") headphones look just like the originals and come with orange and blue ear cushions. New headphones are often wireless these days, but the MDR-3R continues the wired tradition of the MDR-3, with an essential twist: a USB-C connector. For better or worse, the new headphones also use "the same 23 mm driver units as the MDR-3 to reproduce sound quality close to the original," per Sony. Audiophiles will prefer something more advanced, perhaps with additional acoustic features. In addition to the USB-C connector, the MDR-3R also adds an in-line remote control and an integrated microphone. They are available for $60.
